course.title: Thermodynamics and Energy Systems
course.description: How energy moves through engines, power stations, refrigerators and walls, and what limits it. Each lesson practises one engineering judgement: choosing a system, reading a state, testing an efficiency claim, improving a cycle, sizing insulation or checking a power figure.
course.audience: Adults who know specific heat, the ideal gas law, the first law and Carnot efficiency in outline from the Physics II course, and want to work with energy balances, tables and cycles as an engineer does. Logarithms and exponents are used; calculus is not.

paragraphs: How energy moves through engines, power stations, refrigerators and walls, and what limits it. Each lesson practises one engineering judgement: choosing a system, reading a state, testing an efficiency claim, improving a cycle, sizing insulation or checking a power figure.
outcomes: You'll be able to draw a boundary round a real device and write its energy balance.
You'll be able to find the state of water from a table and use enthalpy to size a turbine, pump or condenser.
You'll be able to test an efficiency claim against the Carnot limit and say where a real machine loses work.
You'll be able to analyse steam, gas-turbine, piston-engine and combined cycles and say which change would improve each.
You'll be able to judge a heat pump's COP, a wall's insulation and a power station's heat rate against what the physics allows.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Energy, properties and flow
modules.description: Choosing a system, finding the state of water or a gas, and balancing energy across a device.

modules.title: The second law
modules.description: Why efficiency has a ceiling, and where real machines fall short of it.

modules.title: Power cycles
modules.description: Steam, gas-turbine, piston-engine and combined cycles, and what improves each.

modules.title: Refrigeration and heat transfer
modules.description: Moving heat with work, and how conduction, convection and exchangers set the size of the hardware.

modules.title: Energy systems
modules.description: Reading power-station and capacity-factor data, and comparing ways to heat a building.

concepts.title: System and boundary
concepts.summary: The matter or region you choose to study; the right boundary depends on what you know and what you are asked.

concepts.title: Isolated, closed and open systems
concepts.summary: Isolated: nothing crosses. Closed: heat and work cross but no mass. Open: mass, heat and work all cross.

concepts.title: Heat and work are energy in transit
concepts.summary: A system holds internal, kinetic and potential energy; heat and work exist only as energy crossing the boundary.

concepts.title: Sign convention
concepts.summary: Count heat into the system and work out of the system as positive, and say so before writing a balance.

concepts.title: Saturation
concepts.summary: At a given pressure, liquid and vapour can coexist only at one temperature; the table pairs each saturation temperature with its pressure.

concepts.title: Compressed liquid, mixture, superheated vapour
concepts.summary: Below the saturation temperature at that pressure the water is liquid; at it, a mixture; above it, superheated vapour.

concepts.title: Quality
concepts.summary: Mass of vapour over total mass in the mixture region; h = hf + x hfg.

concepts.title: When the ideal gas model holds
concepts.summary: Pv = RT with absolute temperature and pressure suits gases well above their boiling point at modest pressure, and fails near saturation and at very high pressure (water's critical point is 22.1 MPa).

concepts.title: Enthalpy
concepts.summary: h = u + Pv: the energy a flowing fluid carries across the boundary, including the work of pushing it in.

concepts.title: Steady-flow energy balance
concepts.summary: Per unit mass: h_in + ke_in + pe_in + q = h_out + ke_out + pe_out + w.

concepts.title: Terms you can drop
concepts.summary: In a turbine the kinetic and potential energy changes are under 1 Btu/lbm against hundreds in enthalpy.

concepts.title: Delta h or cp delta T
concepts.summary: Q = m (h_out - h_in) works through a phase change; m cp delta T fails because temperature barely moves while steam condenses.

concepts.title: Throttling
concepts.summary: An ideal throttle valve has h_in = h_out, no work and no heat.

concepts.title: The second law
concepts.summary: No cycle turns all its heat into work, and heat does not flow from cold to hot with no other effect; work can be turned into heat completely.

concepts.title: Carnot efficiency
concepts.summary: eta = 1 - Tc/Th with absolute temperatures; no engine between the same two reservoirs does better.

concepts.title: Practical limits
concepts.summary: The sink is the environment (about 60 F) and the source is capped by materials (about 1,500 F), giving 73.5%; real fossil plants reach about 40%.

concepts.title: Entropy
concepts.summary: A property; for a reversible process delta S = Q / T. It cannot fall around a cycle and measures energy no longer available for work.

concepts.title: Isentropic process
concepts.summary: Reversible and adiabatic; a vertical line on a T-s diagram. A real expansion leans to the right.

concepts.title: Isentropic efficiency
concepts.summary: Turbine: actual work over ideal work. Pump or compressor: ideal work over actual work.

concepts.title: Causes of irreversibility
concepts.summary: Friction, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, and mixing.

concepts.title: The four processes
concepts.summary: Pump (liquid, small work), boiler (heat in at constant pressure), turbine (work out), condenser (heat out at constant pressure).

concepts.title: Thermal efficiency
concepts.summary: Net work over heat in: (w_turbine - w_pump) / (h3 - h2).

concepts.title: Average heat-input temperature
concepts.summary: Raising the average temperature at which heat enters, or lowering the temperature at which it leaves, raises efficiency.

concepts.title: Superheat, reheat, regeneration
concepts.summary: Superheat and reheat also dry the exhaust; regeneration preheats feedwater with bled steam.

concepts.title: Brayton cycle
concepts.summary: Compressor, combustor and turbine; the turbine drives the compressor and the rest of its work is the output.

concepts.title: Ideal efficiency
concepts.summary: eta = 1 - (P_in / P_out)^((gamma - 1)/gamma): it depends on the pressure ratio and gamma, not on the peak temperature.

concepts.title: Pressure-ratio limit
concepts.summary: A higher ratio makes the compressor outlet hotter, which leaves less temperature rise before the turbine's metal limit.

concepts.title: Recuperator
concepts.summary: A heat exchanger that preheats compressed air with exhaust; it only works when the pressure ratio is low.

concepts.title: Otto cycle
concepts.summary: Isentropic compression, constant-volume heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-volume rejection; eta = 1 - 1/r^(gamma-1).

concepts.title: Knock
concepts.summary: A petrol-air mixture that gets too hot during compression ignites early; this caps the compression ratio.

concepts.title: Diesel cycle
concepts.summary: Air is compressed and the fuel ignites by the heat of compression; heat is added at constant pressure, and efficiency also depends on the cut-off ratio.

concepts.title: Turbocharger and supercharger
concepts.summary: A turbocharger recovers exhaust energy; a crankshaft-driven supercharger raises power but not efficiency.

concepts.title: Topping and bottoming cycles
concepts.summary: A gas turbine's hot exhaust raises steam for a second engine, so the same fuel runs two cycles.

concepts.title: Stacked efficiency
concepts.summary: eta_total = eta_top + (1 - eta_top) x eta_bottom; the bottoming cycle works only on what the first one left.

concepts.title: HHV and LHV
concepts.summary: Efficiency quoted on the lower heating value reads higher than on the higher heating value; for methane the two differ by about 11%.

concepts.title: Combined heat and power
concepts.summary: A total that counts both electricity and useful heat is not an electrical efficiency.

concepts.title: Vapour-compression cycle
concepts.summary: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve (throttle, constant enthalpy) and evaporator.

concepts.title: Coefficient of performance
concepts.summary: Useful heat moved over work in; COP_heating = COP_cooling + 1; a resistance heater has COP 1.

concepts.title: Carnot COP
concepts.summary: COP_heating = T_H / (T_H - T_C) with absolute temperatures; real machines reach a fraction of it.

concepts.title: Temperature lift
concepts.summary: COP falls as the gap between source and delivery temperature widens.

concepts.title: Series resistance
concepts.summary: Heat flux = temperature difference over the sum of the layer resistances, each thickness / k.

concepts.title: Convection film
concepts.summary: Q = h A delta T; the film is one more resistance, 1/h; turbulent flow has higher h.

concepts.title: Dominant resistance
concepts.summary: The largest resistance sets the heat flow and takes most of the temperature drop.

concepts.title: Critical radius
concepts.summary: On a small cylinder, insulation below r = k/h raises heat loss.

concepts.title: Parallel flow and counter-flow
concepts.summary: Counter-flow gives a more even temperature difference; the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid's outlet.

concepts.title: Log mean temperature difference
concepts.summary: (delta T2 - delta T1) / ln(delta T2 / delta T1) from the temperature differences at the two ends.

concepts.title: Overall coefficient
concepts.summary: U = 1 / (1/h1 + thickness/k + 1/h2) for a thin wall; Q = U A LMTD.

concepts.title: The smaller h dominates
concepts.summary: Improving the poorer film pays more than improving the better one.

concepts.title: Heat rate
concepts.summary: Fuel energy in Btu per net kWh generated; efficiency = 3,412 / heat rate.

concepts.title: Rejected heat
concepts.summary: Fuel energy minus electricity: for the average coal plant about 68% of the fuel energy.

concepts.title: Fleet average against new-build
concepts.summary: EIA's yearly averages cover the whole running fleet, not the best new plant.

concepts.title: Plausibility check
concepts.summary: A stated efficiency must sit below the Carnot-based ceiling and near the range for that plant type.

concepts.title: Capacity factor
concepts.summary: Energy a unit actually produced over what it would make at full power for the whole period; a measure of use, not of conversion efficiency.

concepts.title: Nameplate to energy
concepts.summary: Annual energy = capacity x 8,760 h x capacity factor.

concepts.title: Primary energy for heat
concepts.summary: Fuel per kWh of heat = (heat rate / 3,412) / COP for a heat pump, or 1 / efficiency for a boiler.

concepts.title: Grid dependence
concepts.summary: Whether a heat pump cuts emissions depends on the grid as well as on its COP.

lessons.title: Where you draw the boundary

lead.text: A **system** is the matter or region you have chosen to study, everything outside it is the **surroundings**, and the surface between the two is the **boundary**. The boundary can be a real wall, such as the casing of a pump, or an imaginary surface drawn across a pipe, and it can be fixed or can move. The handbook behind this course gives three very different examples of a system: water on one side of a heat exchanger, fluid in a length of pipe, and the oil circuit that lubricates a diesel engine.

Nothing in the physics says which of these to choose. The best boundary depends on what you know about the machine and on what you have been asked to find, so one plant can be studied as a single system or as five. Once the boundary is drawn, the first law says that energy is neither created nor destroyed but only changes form, so energy that crosses into the system either crosses out again or stays inside as a change in the stored energy.

Systems are sorted by what is allowed to cross their boundary. In an **isolated system** nothing crosses: no mass, no heat and no work. In a **closed system** no mass crosses, but heat and work may. In an **open system** mass crosses as well, and each kilogram that enters or leaves carries energy with it, so an open system can exchange all three. The figure sets the three side by side, and the table on its right shows which crossings each type allows.

afterFigure.text: A closed system is therefore not the same thing as a sealed, insulated one, which is how the word is often misread. The gas in a piston and cylinder is closed because none of it crosses the cylinder wall, yet the piston does work on it and the wall can pass heat. Most machines in a power plant are open, since fluid flows through them, and the handbook treats the steam plant as a whole as a closed system and each machine inside it as an open one.

diagram.alt: Three sketches of a system inside a dashed boundary, with a table of what may cross it. An isolated system exchanges nothing, a closed one exchanges heat and work, and an open one exchanges mass as well.
diagram.caption: A dashed boundary round each system, and the row of the table that matches. Use the buttons to compare the three.

steps.headline: Heat and work cross the boundary

lead.text: Take the boundary round the feed pump of the plant, as in the figure. Water crosses it at the inlet and at the outlet, which is mass, and each kilogram brings its stored energy in and takes it out again. A shaft from a motor outside the boundary turns the pump, and the energy it delivers is **work**. The casing is a little warmer than the room, so a small amount of energy also crosses because of that temperature difference, and energy that crosses for that reason is **heat**.

afterFigure.text: Both are energy in transit. The handbook is direct about it: systems never possess heat or work, and both are boundary phenomena, seen only as energy crossing the boundary. The water in the pump holds internal, kinetic and potential energy as properties, but it holds no heat and no work, so a hot pipe does not contain heat in the way it contains internal energy. The same view explains why the electricity feeding the motor is missing from this balance: it does not cross the pump's boundary, and only the shaft work does.

diagram.alt: A pump inside a dashed boundary. Water enters and leaves, a shaft from a motor outside the boundary brings work in, and a little heat leaks out through the casing.
diagram.caption: A boundary round the feed pump. Mass, work and heat cross it, and the motor and its electricity stay outside.

cases.label: The pump

lead.text: Once the crossings are listed, each needs a sign. This course counts **heat into the system as positive and work out of the system as positive**, so a boundary round a turbine has positive work, because the turbine does work on the generator, and a boundary round a pump has negative work, because work is done on the pump's water. Heat that leaks out through a casing is negative heat. The convention is the one in the [[first law|Energy is conserved: change in internal energy equals heat in minus work out. Met in 'Gases and the first law'.]] of Physics II, $\Delta U = Q - W$, where work done by the system is positive.

afterFigure.text: A different convention, such as counting work done on the system as positive, is equally valid, and what matters is that you state the convention before writing a balance and keep to it. A wrong sign is the most common way for a correct list of crossings to produce a wrong answer. The handbook says that its own choice is made 'for convenience and as a standard convention'.

steps.headline: Give each crossing its sign for a boundary round a steam turbine that delivers 5,000 kW to a generator and loses 80 kW of heat through its casing.

workedSteps.text: Draw the boundary round the casing. Steam crosses at the inlet and the outlet, so the system is open. The two steam flows carry energy with them, which later lessons handle with enthalpy, and the direction of each arrow already says whether it enters or leaves.
The shaft turns the generator, so the turbine puts work into the surroundings. Work out of the system is positive.
The casing is warmer than the room, so energy leaves it as heat. Heat into the system is positive, so heat out is negative.
Both terms now sit in the balance on the side they belong to, and the first law reads: energy brought in by the steam, plus $Q$, equals energy carried out by the steam, plus $W$.

steps.headline: Give each crossing its sign for a boundary round a feed pump that takes 6 kW of shaft power and loses 0.3 kW of heat through its casing.

workedSteps.text: Water crosses at the inlet and at the outlet, so the pump is an open system.
The shaft puts work into the water. Choose the work term.
The casing passes 0.3 kW of heat to the room. Find the heat term.

lead.text: The figure draws the same plant three times. With the boundary round the pump alone, water crosses at both ends, the shaft brings work in and a little heat leaks out, so the pump is an open system. Round the turbine alone, steam crosses at both ends and the shaft takes work out, which is again an open system. Draw the boundary round all four machines and the water never crosses it, because only heat at the boiler, heat at the condenser and the two shafts do, so the loop is a closed system.

afterFigure.text: The two choices answer different questions. The pump boundary gives the pump's work from the water's state going in and coming out. The loop boundary gives the plant's net work from the heat taken in and the heat rejected, with no knowledge of the steam between the machines. Which to choose depends on which quantities you know and which you want to find.

reveal.text: Only the flows that reach through the boundary count. The exhaust passing from turbine to condenser is internal and drops out of the balance, while the steam entering the turbine and the water leaving the condenser cross it.
Oil enters and leaves, so mass crosses, and the heat it gives up crosses the tube walls. The handbook uses the fluid on one side of a heat exchanger as one of its own examples of a system.

lessons.orientation: Choose a system and boundary for a real device, classify it as isolated, closed or open, and list what crosses the boundary as mass, heat or work.
lessons.nextAction: Place water in the right region from its temperature and pressure, and read its enthalpy from a table.

blocks.text: A steam power plant circulates one stock of water through four machines. The boiler adds heat to it, the turbine takes work out of it, the condenser removes heat from it, and the pump raises its pressure again before it returns to the boiler. To find the power the pump needs, an engineer does not have to follow the water through the other three machines, because she can draw a line round the pump alone and account for what crosses that line.

Where the line is drawn decides which quantities enter the balance, and each choice of line gives a different list of crossings for the same plant. Choosing it well is the first step of every calculation in this course.

intro.promise: By the end you'll choose a boundary for a real machine, call it isolated, closed or open, and list what crosses it as mass, heat or work with the right signs.
intro.whyItMatters: Every energy balance in this course starts from a boundary and a list of what crosses it.

recap.keyIdea: Choose the boundary to fit what you know and what you want to find, call it isolated, closed or open by what crosses it, and sign each crossing with heat in and work out positive.

blocks.text: A system is the matter or region you choose to study, and its boundary decides which crossings appear in the balance. A boundary with nothing crossing is [[isolated|Nothing crosses: no mass, heat or work. Met in 'Isolated, closed and open'.]], one with heat and work but no mass is closed, and one with mass as well is open, so a turbine or a pump is open while the whole steam loop is closed.

Heat and work are energy in transit and are never stored in a system. With heat in and work out counted as positive, a turbine's work is positive, a pump's work is negative and heat leaking through a casing is negative.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson fixes the state of the water inside a boundary, because no balance can be written until you know whether that water is liquid, vapour or a mixture of the two.

lessons.title: Which state is this?

lead.text: Heat a pan of water on a stove with the lid off, so that the pressure stays at the atmosphere's 101.32 kPa, and its temperature goes through three stages. It rises while the water is liquid, holds at 100 °C while the water boils away, and rises again once all of it has become vapour. The figure plots temperature against **specific enthalpy**, the energy that each kilogram of the water carries, measured from water at 0 °C. The next lesson says what enthalpy contains, and for now it is the quantity that steam tables list and the one along the horizontal axis.

afterFigure.text: The flat stretch is where liquid and vapour exist together. At a given pressure that can happen at only one temperature, the **saturation temperature**, which is 100 °C at 101.32 kPa, and read the other way 101.32 kPa is the **saturation pressure** at 100 °C. The stretch is long, because boiling water that is already at 100 °C takes 2,256.3 kJ/kg, against 335.2 kJ/kg to warm it from 20 °C to 100 °C. That 2,256.3 kJ/kg is the [[latent heat|Heat absorbed or released at constant temperature while a substance changes phase. Met in 'Heat and temperature'.]] of vaporisation that Physics II gave as about 2,260 kJ/kg.
On either side of the stretch the water is in one phase. Liquid colder than the saturation temperature for its pressure is **compressed liquid**, and vapour hotter than it is **superheated vapour**.

diagram.alt: Temperature against specific enthalpy for water heated at 101.32 kPa: a rising line while the water is liquid, a flat line at 100 degrees while it boils, and a rising line again as vapour. One stretch is highlighted in each view.

lead.text: A steam table gives, for each saturation temperature, the saturation pressure and the enthalpy at the two ends of the flat stretch. The enthalpy of **saturated liquid**, water at the point of boiling, is written $h_f$, the extra enthalpy needed to turn it completely into vapour is $h_{fg}$, and the enthalpy of **saturated vapour** is therefore $h_g = h_f + h_{fg}$. The table used here lists $h_f$ as the enthalpy of the liquid and $h_{fg}$ as the heat of vaporisation, in J/g, which is the same as kJ/kg, and the figure shows four of its rows with $h_g$ added.

afterFigure.text: The table also settles the region. Look up the saturation pressure at the water's temperature. If the water's pressure is higher, it is compressed liquid, because it is under more pressure than it needs in order to boil at that temperature. If the pressure is lower, it is superheated vapour, and if the two are equal the water can be saturated liquid, saturated vapour or a mixture of the two. At 200 °C the saturation pressure is 1,554.3 kPa, so water at 200 °C is compressed liquid above that pressure and superheated vapour below it.

lead.text: Inside the flat stretch the temperature and the pressure are tied together by the saturation curve, so they cannot say how far along the stretch the water has got. A third property does that. The **quality**, $x$, is the mass of vapour divided by the total mass of liquid and vapour, so $x = 0$ is saturated liquid and $x = 1$ is saturated vapour, and the **moisture** is the remaining fraction, $1 - x$. The handbook is explicit that quality has meaning only in the saturated state.

afterFigure.text: Enthalpy is shared out between the two phases in proportion to their masses, so a mixture has $h = h_f + x\,h_{fg}$: start from the liquid's enthalpy and add the fraction $x$ of the amount needed to vaporise it. At 200 °C a mixture with $x = 0.90$ has $h = 851.9 + 0.90 \times 1{,}937.3 = 2{,}595$ kJ/kg. Run the other way, a measured enthalpy gives the quality, $x = (h - h_f)/h_{fg}$. Outside the flat stretch quality has no meaning, and a compressed liquid or a superheated vapour needs its temperature and pressure, which are independent there.

reveal.text: Two independent properties normally fix a state, and inside the mixture region temperature and pressure are not independent, which is why the quality has to be given as well.

steps.headline: Find the specific enthalpy of wet steam at 100 °C and 101.32 kPa with a quality of 0.90.

workedSteps.text: Check the region. The saturation pressure at 100 °C is 101.32 kPa, so the pair is a saturated state and quality applies.
Read the table at 100 °C.
Start from the liquid's enthalpy and add 90% of the amount needed to vaporise it.
Add the two parts.
As a check, the result lies between $h_f = 419.0$ and $h_g = 2{,}675.3$ kJ/kg, as the enthalpy of any mixture at this pressure must.

steps.headline: Find the quality of wet steam at 200 °C whose specific enthalpy is 2,400 kJ/kg.

workedSteps.text: At 200 °C the table gives $h_f = 851.9$ and $h_{fg} = 1{,}937.3$ kJ/kg, so $h_g = 2{,}789.2$ kJ/kg. Since 2,400 lies between $h_f$ and $h_g$, the steam is a mixture.
Rearrange $h = h_f + x\,h_{fg}$ to find $x$. The enthalpy above the liquid's value is divided by one of the table's numbers. Choose it.
Work out the quality.

lead.text: A gas law is written for pressures and temperatures counted from true zero. A pressure gauge reads from the surrounding atmosphere, so the **absolute pressure** that the law needs is the gauge reading plus the atmospheric pressure, about 101.3 kPa. The Celsius scale puts its zero at the freezing point of water, so the **absolute temperature** is the Celsius value plus 273, in kelvin, which is the handbook's rounding of 273.15. Both conversions are made before any number goes into $Pv = RT$.

afterFigure.text: A sealed rigid cylinder of air shows how much depends on them. Its volume and its mass are fixed, so its absolute pressure rises in proportion to its absolute temperature, and the handbook states that a 5% rise in absolute temperature gives a 5% rise in absolute pressure. If the gauge reads 200 kPa at 20 °C, the cylinder holds 301.3 kPa at 293 K. Heated to 80 °C, which is 353 K, it holds 301.3 × 353/293 = 363.0 kPa, and the gauge reads 261.7 kPa. Scaling the gauge reading itself would give 241 kPa, and scaling by the Celsius figures would give 800 kPa, which are both wrong.

lead.text: The ideal gas law, $Pv = RT$, where $v$ is the volume of one kilogram and $R$ is the gas constant of that gas, describes molecules so far apart that they neither attract one another nor condense. No real gas obeys it completely. Near its boiling point a small rise in pressure makes a gas condense, with a drastic fall in volume, and at very high pressure the forces between molecules matter. The model is safe for a gas well above its saturation temperature at modest pressure, such as air at room conditions, and unsafe close to saturation or near water's critical point, 22.1 MPa at 374 °C.

afterFigure.text: The steam table lets you test the model on steam itself. With $R = 0.4615$ kJ/(kg K), which is the universal gas constant divided by the molar mass of water, 18.015 g/mol, $Pv = RT$ gives a density of 0.588 kg/m³ for saturated steam at 100 °C, against 0.5974 in the table, which is 1.5% low. At 200 °C and 1,554.3 kPa it gives 7.12 against 7.868, which is 9.5% low. In a condenser at 40 °C and 7.4 kPa the error is only 0.1%, so the same fluid is a good ideal gas in one place and a poor one in another. A value taken from air does not carry over either: steam's heat capacity ratio is 1.324 at 100 °C, against 1.4 for air.

lessons.orientation: Place water in the right region from its temperature and pressure, read enthalpy from a saturation table or from quality, and judge whether an ideal gas model is safe.
lessons.nextAction: Write the steady-flow energy balance for a turbine, a condenser and a valve.

blocks.text: A pan of water at 100 °C might hold liquid, a mixture of liquid and vapour, or vapour. All three are common, and their enthalpies differ by thousands of kilojoules per kilogram, so an energy balance on a boiler, a turbine or a condenser cannot start until you know which one it is. The temperature alone often cannot say, because the answer depends on the pressure, and in one region on a third property.

Engineers settle this with a steam table, which pairs each boiling temperature with its pressure and enthalpies, and with a judgement about whether a simple gas law is accurate enough for the fluid in front of them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll place water in its region from its temperature and pressure, read its enthalpy from a table or from its quality, and judge whether an ideal gas model is safe.
intro.whyItMatters: A balance on a boiler, turbine or condenser needs to know the state of the water before any of its energy figures mean anything.

recap.keyIdea: Compare the water's pressure with the saturation pressure at its temperature to find its region, use the quality in $h = h_f + x\,h_{fg}$ inside the mixture, and put absolute values into $Pv = RT$ only for a gas that is well away from saturation.

blocks.text: The saturation table pairs each temperature with the [[saturation pressure|The one pressure at which liquid and vapour coexist at that temperature. Met in 'Heating water at constant pressure'.]] and the enthalpies $h_f$ and $h_{fg}$. A pressure above the saturation pressure at the water's temperature means compressed liquid, one below it means superheated vapour, and in the mixture between them the quality $x$ is the vapour fraction.

The ideal gas law needs absolute pressure, which is gauge plus atmosphere, and absolute temperature, which is kelvin. It is accurate for air at room conditions and falls 10% short for saturated steam at 1,554.3 kPa, so a gas near saturation or at high pressure is checked against a table before the model is trusted.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these enthalpies to write the energy balance for a turbine, a condenser and a valve.

lessons.title: The energy balance on a device

lead.text: Take the boundary round a turbine, as in the first lesson, and list what crosses it. The steam carries its internal energy across, together with kinetic energy from its speed and potential energy from its height. There is one more item that a closed system does not have. To push each kilogram of steam into the turbine against the pressure inside, the fluid behind it does work, and this **flow work**, $Pv$, crosses the boundary with the steam and leaves with it. Heat and shaft work are the remaining crossings.

afterFigure.text: Internal energy and flow work always travel together across the boundary of an open system, so they are given one name. The **enthalpy**, $h = u + Pv$, is the energy that a kilogram of fluid carries across a boundary, apart from its kinetic and potential energy. The handbook defines it for this reason, since the two terms occur so often in open-system analysis, and it is why steam tables list enthalpy.

lead.text: A turbine in normal running is in **steady state**: the properties at each point do not change with time, so nothing accumulates inside the boundary, and the mass flow in equals the mass flow out. A fixed region of space chosen for a balance of this kind is called a **control volume**. Dividing the energy balance by the mass flow gives it per kilogram of fluid, with [[heat in and work out counted as positive|The convention of this course: heat into the system and work out of it are positive. Met in 'A sign convention'.]]:

afterFigure.text: The subscripts 1 and 2 mean the inlet and the outlet, $V$ is the speed, $z$ is the height above a chosen level, and $q$ and $w$ are the heat and the work for each kilogram. In words, the enthalpy, kinetic energy and potential energy that each kilogram brings in, plus the heat it receives, equal what it takes out, plus the work it delivers. A pump has the same balance with a negative $w$, and a condenser has $w = 0$ because no shaft crosses its boundary.

steps.headline: Find the work done by each kilogram of steam in a turbine.

workedSteps.text: Write the balance per kilogram, with the outlet as the zero of height.
The heat leaves the system, so $q = -12$ kJ/kg. Convert the speed and height terms from J/kg to kJ/kg by dividing by 1,000.
Substitute the numbers.
Solve for the work.
As a check, leaving out the speed and height terms gives 3,138 − 2,559 − 12 = 567 kJ/kg, which differs by 1.9 kJ/kg.

lead.text: Steam enters the turbine at 3,138 kJ/kg and 50 m/s, 2 m above the outlet, and leaves at 2,559 kJ/kg and 80 m/s. The casing loses 12 kJ of heat for each kilogram. These are the handbook's turbine figures, 1,349 and 1,100 Btu/lbm, converted to SI units.

The two views in the figure show that turbine with the speed and height terms left out and put in. The enthalpy of each kilogram falls by 579 kJ, and the two terms together change the work by only 1.9 kJ, which is 0.3% of the answer and too thin to see on a bar drawn to scale. The handbook reaches the same conclusion from its own example, where both changes come to less than 1 Btu/lbm, about 2.3 kJ/kg.

afterFigure.text: A term can be dropped when it is small beside the largest term that stays, and that is a judgement made for each machine, since no rule about turbines settles it. In a nozzle, whose job is to turn enthalpy into speed, the kinetic energy term is the whole point and must stay. A pump or a condenser has a negligible speed change but a work or heat term of its own that cannot go. Check the size of a term against the biggest term in the balance before leaving it out.

lead.text: The same balance describes a pump. Water passes through with almost no change in speed or height, no heat of consequence crosses, and the shaft puts work in, so the pump's work for each kilogram is the rise in enthalpy and is negative. In a steam plant it is small: the energy that the feed pump needs is only 1% to 3% of the turbine's output.

A throttle valve is different again. It drops the pressure of a fluid by forcing it through a partly closed passage, no shaft crosses it, and the process is taken to be adiabatic, so the balance leaves $h_1 = h_2$. The handbook defines a **throttling** process in these terms: no change in enthalpy, no work and no heat. The expansion valve of a refrigerator is an example, in which the pressure falls abruptly while the enthalpy stays constant.

reveal.text: A throttle gives no work and no heat, so the enthalpy before and after the valve is the same. The pressure and the temperature of the fluid both change.

lead.text: A condenser has two fluids, and the balance is written for one at a time. The handbook's condenser takes 2.0 × 10⁶ kg/h of steam, which is 556 kg/s, entering as saturated vapour at 40 °C with $h = 2{,}574$ kJ/kg and leaving as liquid at 30 °C with $h = 125.8$ kJ/kg. Cooling water enters at 18 °C with $h = 75.6$ kJ/kg and, because of an environmental limit on the discharge, may leave at no more than 25 °C, with $h = 104.9$ kJ/kg. No shaft crosses either side and the speed and height changes are small, so each side's balance reduces to $Q = \dot m\,(h_{out} - h_{in})$.

afterFigure.text: Heat leaves the steam and enters the water, so the two are equal in size and opposite in sign, and the condenser moves energy without destroying any. The steam gives up 2,448.2 kJ for each kilogram and each kilogram of water gains 29.3 kJ, so the water flow is 83.6 times the steam flow. The expression $\dot m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ cannot take the place of the enthalpy difference here, because the steam's temperature does not change while it condenses, which leaves $\Delta T$ at zero for most of the heat. Using it on the 10 K of subcooling alone gives $4.18 \times 10 = 42$ kJ/kg, which is 1.7% of the real 2,448 kJ/kg.

steps.headline: Find the cooling water that the handbook's condenser needs.

workedSteps.text: Treat each side as an open system with no shaft. The heat lost by the steam equals the heat gained by the water.
Find the rate at which the steam gives up heat.
Each kilogram of water gains the difference of its two enthalpies.
Divide the heat by the gain per kilogram to find the water flow.

lead.text: The steam flows at 555.6 kg/s and its enthalpy falls from 2,574 to 125.8 kJ/kg, while each kilogram of cooling water gains 29.3 kJ.

reveal.text: The heat to be removed is fixed by the steam, so the water flow is that heat divided by what each kilogram carries away. Allowing a warmer discharge cuts the flow from 46,400 kg/s to about 27,200 kg/s.

lessons.orientation: Write the steady-flow energy balance for a turbine, pump, condenser, heat exchanger or valve, drop the terms that do not matter, and solve for the unknown work, heat or flow.
lessons.reviewLabel: The energy balance on a device
lessons.nextAction: Test a claimed efficiency against the Carnot limit and say which limits come from the second law.

blocks.text: A steam turbine takes in steam that carries 3,100 kJ of energy for each kilogram and sends out steam that carries 2,500 kJ for each kilogram. Whatever energy disappears from the steam has gone somewhere, and the first law says where: some may leak through the casing as heat, and the rest becomes work on the shaft.
An engineer who can write that balance for a turbine can write it for a pump, a condenser or a valve, because each of them reduces to a few terms once she decides which ones can be left out.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the steady-flow energy balance for a turbine, pump, condenser or valve, drop the terms that are small, and solve for the work, heat or flow.
intro.whyItMatters: Sizing a turbine, a pump or a condenser starts from this balance.

recap.keyIdea: For a machine in steady flow, each kilogram brings in enthalpy, kinetic and potential energy plus heat and takes out the same kinds plus work, and the terms that are small beside the largest can be dropped.

blocks.text: The [[enthalpy|The energy a flowing kilogram of fluid carries across a boundary, $h = u + Pv$. Met in 'What crosses a flowing boundary'.]] of a fluid includes the flow work that pushes it across the boundary, so a turbine delivers the enthalpy it loses, less any heat lost and the change in kinetic and potential energy, and a pump or a compressor is the same balance with the work reversed. An ideal throttle valve has no work and no heat, so its enthalpy is the same before and after.

In a condenser the heat lost by the steam is the heat gained by the water, and it is found from $\dot m\,\Delta h$, because $\dot m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ misses the latent heat. Speed and height terms can go when they are small beside the enthalpy change, as in a turbine, and must stay when they are the purpose of the machine, as in a nozzle.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what the first law allows to what the second law forbids, and tests a claimed efficiency against the limit.

lessons.title: Testing a claimed efficiency

lead.text: The first law says that energy is conserved, and it says nothing about direction. It would allow an engine to take 100 kJ from a hot source and turn all of it into work, and it would allow heat to pass from a colder body to a hotter one with nothing else changing. Neither has ever been seen, and the **second law** is the statement of that. Max Planck's form of it is about engines: it is impossible to build an engine that works in a complete cycle and has no effect other than raising a weight and cooling a heat reservoir. R. Clausius stated it for heat in 1850: no device that works in a cycle can do nothing except take heat from a cold body and deliver it to a hotter one.

afterFigure.text: An engine that runs in a cycle must therefore reject some of the heat it takes in to something colder, and only the difference can become work. The handbook states the asymmetry plainly: work can be converted completely into heat, as friction does, but heat supplied to a cycle can never be converted completely into work, however perfectly the engine is designed.

diagram.alt: Two engines between a hot source and a cold sink with arrows sized by energy. One takes in 100 kJ, delivers 40 kJ of work and rejects 60 kJ. The other takes in 100 kJ and delivers all 100 kJ as work, marked as ruled out by the second law.

lead.text: Sadi Carnot, in 1824, gave the second law its practical form. His principle has three parts. No engine can beat a reversible engine working between the same two reservoirs. All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency. And that efficiency depends only on the temperatures of the source and the sink, so that $\eta = 1 - T_C/T_H$, the [[Carnot efficiency|The greatest efficiency possible between two reservoirs, one minus the ratio of their absolute temperatures. Met in 'Engines and the limit'.]], where $T_C$ and $T_H$ are the absolute temperatures of the sink and the source.

afterFigure.text: The temperatures must be absolute. Between a 540 °C source and a 30 °C sink the limit is $1 - 303/813 = 62.7\%$, whereas the Celsius figures would give $1 - 30/540 = 94.4\%$, a limit that no engine could approach. Because real machines have friction and cannot be made reversible, the handbook calls the Carnot efficiency an unattainable upper limit: the actual efficiency of a real system is always below it.

lead.text: A claim of efficiency can be tested in three steps: convert the two temperatures to kelvin, work out the Carnot limit, and compare the claim with it. A claim above the limit is impossible, however the engine is built. A claim below the limit is allowed by the second law, and the next question is how far below. Real engines fall well short of their limit, because friction and other losses stop them being reversible, so a claim that sits close to the limit deserves a second look even though the law allows it. The figure shows the datasheet claim from the opening of this lesson on a graph, and three claims with their limits in a table.

afterFigure.text: The test needs only the claim and the two temperatures, so it can be applied to a machine that you know nothing else about. It sorts claims into three groups, as the table shows: impossible, if they exceed the limit, doubtful, if they are allowed but sit close to the limit, and plausible, if they fall well inside it.

steps.headline: Test a datasheet claim of 38% for an engine working from a 600 °C source to a 25 °C sink.

workedSteps.text: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
Work out the Carnot limit.
Compare the claim with the limit. It is below, so the second law allows it.
Find how far below. The claim is 58% of the limit, which leaves plenty of room for the losses of a real engine, so the claim is plausible.

steps.headline: Compare the handbook's steam cycle, which reaches 18.0%, with its Carnot limit.

workedSteps.text: Convert to kelvin. The source is at 171 °C and the sink at 16 °C.
Work out the Carnot limit.
Compare the actual efficiency with the limit as a share of it.

lead.text: The formula says that a higher efficiency needs a hotter source or a colder sink, and the limits on the two come from different places. The second law sets the form of the cap and keeps it below 100%. The environment sets the sink: heat is finally rejected to the earth, and the handbook fixes that sink at about 60 °F, which is 289 K or 16 °C. The source is set by fuel and by materials. Fuel can burn at about 1,670 °C, but boilers cannot hold steam that hot, and the handbook limits them to about 1,500 °F, which is 1,089 K or 816 °C.

afterFigure.text: Those two limits give a ceiling of $1 - 289/1{,}089 = 73.5\%$ for any steam plant, whatever its design. Real plants fall well short of it. The handbook gives typical efficiencies of about 40% for fossil plants and about 31% for nuclear plants, which are 54% and 42% of the ceiling, so real plants reach roughly half of what the law and the environment allow. Raising the ceiling means raising the source temperature, and that depends on better metals.

reveal.text: Materials limit the source and the environment limits the sink. The second law only fixes how the efficiency depends on the two.

lessons.orientation: Compute the Carnot limit between two temperatures, use it to test a claimed efficiency, and say which limits come from the second law and which from materials and the environment.
lessons.nextAction: Find where real machines lose work, using entropy and the isentropic efficiency.

blocks.text: A datasheet for a steam engine claims that it turns 38% of the heat from a 600 °C source into work while rejecting heat to air at 25 °C. An engineer deciding whether to believe it can test the claim without knowing anything about the engine's design, because the second law of thermodynamics caps the efficiency of every engine that works between two temperatures.

The cap is a short formula, and the skill lies in using it: converting to absolute temperatures, comparing the claim with the cap, and judging a claim that falls below the cap as well as one that rises above it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out the Carnot limit between two temperatures, test a claimed efficiency against it, and say which limits come from the second law and which from the environment and materials.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you check an efficiency claim on the back of an envelope, before any design work.

recap.keyIdea: The second law caps every engine at the Carnot efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$ in absolute temperatures, so a claim above it is impossible, one far below it is plausible, and the ceilings in practice come from the environment and from materials.

blocks.text: The second law forbids a cycle that turns all of its heat into work, and Carnot's principle gives the cap for any engine between two reservoirs. To test a claim, convert the temperatures to kelvin, work out $1 - T_C/T_H$ and compare: above it is impossible, and below it is allowed but doubtful if it sits close to the limit, since real engines reach roughly half of theirs.

The law fixes only the form of the limit. The sink is the environment, at about 16 °C, and the source is held to about 816 °C by boiler metals, which gives a ceiling of 73.5% for a steam plant against about 40% for real fossil plants.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks inside the real machines to see where they lose work, using entropy and the isentropic efficiency of a turbine and a pump.

lessons.title: Where real machines lose work

lead.text: The ideal expansion of steam in a turbine is both reversible and adiabatic, and a process of that kind is **isentropic**, which means that its [[entropy|The property whose change is the heat transferred in a reversible process divided by the absolute temperature, $Q/T$. Met in 'Engines and the limit'.]] stays the same. The handbook calls entropy a measure of how much heat is unavailable for doing work in a cycle. On a diagram of temperature against entropy the ideal expansion is a vertical line, because the entropy does not change along it.

afterFigure.text: A real expansion between the same two pressures looks much the same, but its line slants slightly to the right, since the entropy increases from the start of the process to the end. The lean is a picture of the losses: friction in the blades, leakage past them and, to a lesser extent, friction in the bearings. A turbine that creates less entropy gets closer to ideal.

diagram.alt: A temperature entropy diagram with a high pressure line and a low pressure line. An ideal expansion drops vertically from state 1 to state 2s, and a real expansion leans to the right to state 2a, which has gained entropy.
diagram.caption: A turbine expansion between two pressures. Use the buttons to add the real expansion to the ideal one.

lead.text: To say how good a real turbine is, compare it with the ideal turbine that expands the same steam from the same inlet state to the same exhaust pressure. The **isentropic efficiency** of a turbine is the actual work divided by the work of the isentropic turbine, and when the heat loss is small each work is an enthalpy drop, so $\eta_t = (h_1 - h_{2a})/(h_1 - h_{2s})$. Here $h_{2s}$ is the exit enthalpy of the ideal expansion and $h_{2a}$ is the actual exit enthalpy.

afterFigure.text: The handbook reads an ideal expansion from a steam chart: superheated steam at about 4.8 MPa and 360 °C expanded at constant entropy to about 965 kPa falls in enthalpy from about 3,100 to 2,740 kJ/kg, an ideal drop of 360 kJ/kg. A real turbine ends at a higher enthalpy, because less work was taken out. For small turbines the handbook gives an isentropic efficiency of 60% to 80%, and for large turbines about 90%.

steps.headline: Find the isentropic efficiency of a turbine in which steam enters at 3,100 kJ/kg and leaves at 2,838 kJ/kg, where the ideal exit would be at 2,740 kJ/kg.

workedSteps.text: Find the work of the ideal turbine, the drop to the ideal exit.
Find the work of the real turbine, the drop to the real exit.
Divide the actual work by the ideal work.
Compare with the typical values. At 0.73 the turbine fits the 60% to 80% of a small machine, and it would be low for a large one.

lead.text: The ideal exit comes from the handbook's steam-chart example, converted to SI units. The real exit is an illustrative figure.

steps.headline: Find the exit enthalpy when the same steam expands through a turbine with an isentropic efficiency of 0.85.

workedSteps.text: The ideal expansion delivers 360 kJ/kg, from 3,100 down to 2,740 kJ/kg.
Find the work the real turbine delivers.
With no heat loss, the work is the enthalpy drop. Find the exit enthalpy.

reveal.text: A real pump needs more work than an ideal one, so its efficiency is the ideal work divided by the actual work. The handbook defines pump efficiency that way, and it keeps the figure below 1.

lead.text: A pump or a compressor has the ratio the other way up. A real one needs more work than an ideal one, so the **pump efficiency** is the ideal work divided by the actual work, $\eta_p = w_{ideal}/w_{actual}$, and it cannot exceed 1. Since the work is the rise in enthalpy, the actual exit enthalpy is $h_{out,a} = h_{in} + (h_{out,s} - h_{in})/\eta_p$, where $h_{out,s}$ is the exit enthalpy of the ideal pump. The isentropic efficiency of a compressor has the same form.

afterFigure.text: Take a feed pump of 75% efficiency, as in the handbook's example, with water entering at 40 °C and $h = 167.2$ kJ/kg, where an ideal pump would raise the enthalpy by 5.0 kJ/kg. The real pump raises it by $5.0/0.75 = 6.7$ kJ/kg, so the water leaves at 173.9 kJ/kg, and the extra 1.7 kJ/kg ends as thermal energy in the water. Beside the 262 kJ/kg of the turbine above, 6.7 kJ/kg is about 2.5%, which is within the 1% to 3% of the turbine's output that a feed pump takes in a steam plant.

lead.text: The lean on the diagram is entropy created inside the machine, and the handbook names four common causes of irreversibility: friction, a fluid expanding without restraint, heat flowing across a finite gap in temperature, and the mixing of unlike substances. Each can be found in a steam plant. Water rubbing along a long pipe is friction. Gas released into an empty tank expands without restraint, so its pressure falls and it does no work. A flame heating a boiler tube transfers heat across a gap of hundreds of kelvin, and fuel and air meeting in a burner are mixed.

afterFigure.text: Every real device has some of these, and each costs work in the same way: it creates entropy, which shows as the lean of the real line on the diagram and as an exit enthalpy above the ideal. The four are also the places to look when a machine falls short, because a designer reduces each loss by attacking its cause.

lessons.orientation: Compute the isentropic efficiency of a turbine or pump from enthalpies, read an ideal and a real process on a T-s diagram, and name the cause of an irreversibility.
lessons.nextAction: Trace a steam cycle and decide which change would raise its efficiency.

blocks.text: The ideal expansion of steam between two pressures would deliver a certain amount of work, and a real turbine always delivers less. The first law says that the missing energy cannot be destroyed, so it has to be somewhere, and the second law says why a real machine always misses some: the machine creates entropy, and the energy that would have been work leaves in the exhaust instead.

Engineers turn that into a single number that compares a real turbine or pump with the ideal one that would do the same job. Reading it correctly shows where a machine loses work and whether a quoted figure is believable.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out the isentropic efficiency of a turbine or pump from its enthalpies, read an ideal and a real expansion on a T-s diagram, and name the cause of an irreversibility.
intro.whyItMatters: It tells you which machine in a plant is worth improving and how much an upgrade could gain.

recap.keyIdea: A real turbine ends at a higher enthalpy than the isentropic one because entropy is created inside it, its efficiency is the actual work over the ideal work, and a pump or compressor is the reverse.

blocks.text: On a T-s diagram the ideal expansion is vertical and the real one leans to the right by the entropy that friction, leakage and other irreversibilities create. The [[isentropic efficiency|Actual work divided by the work of the ideal isentropic machine, for a turbine. Met in 'Isentropic efficiency'.]] of a turbine is $(h_1 - h_{2a})/(h_1 - h_{2s})$, about 60% to 80% for small turbines and about 90% for large ones, and the missing work stays in the steam as a higher exit enthalpy.

A pump or compressor needs more work than the ideal one, so its efficiency is the ideal work divided by the actual work. Irreversibility has four usual sources: friction, unrestrained expansion, heat flowing across a large temperature gap and mixing. An upgrade is worth most where the ideal work is largest, which is why a turbine matters far more than a feed pump.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses these ideas to trace the steam cycle and decide which change would raise a plant's efficiency.

lessons.title: Reading and improving a steam cycle

lead.text: The loop in the figure has four devices, and the water is numbered at each place where it enters or leaves one. Saturated liquid leaves the condenser at state 1 and goes to the pump, which raises its pressure and delivers it at state 2. The boiler adds heat at constant pressure until the water is steam at state 3, the turbine expands that steam down to the condenser pressure at state 4 and delivers work, and the condenser removes heat at constant pressure until the water is a saturated liquid again at state 1.

The ideal version of this loop is the **Rankine cycle**, which carries the name of William John Macquorn Rankine, a Scottish professor at Glasgow University. In it the pump and the turbine are [[isentropic|Reversible and with no heat exchange, so the entropy stays constant. Met in 'Where real machines lose work'.]], which draws the compression from 1 to 2 and the expansion from 3 to 4 as vertical lines on a temperature-entropy diagram and leaves the boiler and the condenser as the only places where heat crosses the boundary.

afterFigure.text: Only the pump handles *liquid*, and a liquid needs little energy to be raised to a higher pressure. In a real plant the feed pump takes only 1 to 3% of the turbine's output, so the efficiency of the plant is decided almost entirely by what happens to the steam.

reveal.text: The rise in enthalpy from state 1 to state 2 is the pump's work, and it is small because the water stays liquid. The next screen puts a number on it.

lead.text: Each device is a control volume with one stream in and one stream out, so the [[steady-flow energy balance|The heat and work a device takes in balance the change in enthalpy of the stream through it. Met in 'The energy balance on a device'.]] gives its heat or work as a difference of enthalpies. Per kilogram of water, the pump takes $w_p = h_2 - h_1$, the boiler adds $q_{in} = h_3 - h_2$, the turbine delivers $w_t = h_3 - h_4$ and the condenser removes $q_{out} = h_4 - h_1$.

The **thermal efficiency** of the cycle compares what you *get* with what you *pay for*. You get the net work, which is the turbine's work less the pump's, and you pay for the heat the boiler adds, so $\eta = (w_t - w_p) / q_{in}$. The figure lists one set of states. Only $h_1$ comes from a table, the 167.2 kJ/kg of saturated liquid at 40 °C and 7.37 kPa, and the other three are illustrative values of the right size for a plant, because exact ones would need a superheated-steam table.

afterFigure.text: Because the cycle returns to state 1, the net work must also equal the heat added less the heat removed, $q_{in} - q_{out}$. That gives a second way to find it, and a check on the first.

steps.headline: Find the thermal efficiency of a cycle with h1 = 167.2, h2 = 182.0, h3 = 3,400 and h4 = 2,200 kJ/kg.

workedSteps.text: The pump work is the rise in enthalpy across the pump.
The turbine work is the fall in enthalpy across the turbine.
The water enters the boiler after the pump, so the boiler's heat is measured from $h_2$, not from $h_1$.
The net work is the turbine's work less the pump's.
The efficiency is the net work divided by the heat added.
As a check, the condenser removes $h_4 - h_1 = 2032.8$ kJ/kg, and the heat added less the heat removed gives the same net work.
Real single-cycle steam plants reach 35 to 42%, so 36.8% is a believable size, and the pump took only $14.8 / 1200 = 1.2\%$ of the turbine's work.

steps.headline: Find the thermal efficiency of cycle B, which has the same pump and condenser but h3 = 3,500 and h4 = 2,250 kJ/kg.

workedSteps.text: The pump and the condenser are unchanged, so the pump work is again $h_2 - h_1$. Cycle B's higher enthalpies are illustrative values too.
The turbine now has a larger enthalpy drop.
Choose the heat the boiler adds to each kilogram.
The net work is the turbine's work less the pump's.
Divide the net work by the heat added to find the efficiency.
Cycle B comes out about 0.4 points above the first cycle, and its size is still inside the 35 to 42% of real plants.

reveal.text: A liquid is hard to compress, so the pump that feeds a boiler is small beside the turbine, and a sheet that shows otherwise is worth rechecking before any efficiency is quoted.

lead.text: On a temperature-entropy diagram the heat added in a reversible process is the area under its path, measured down to absolute zero. In the figure the area under the heating path from 2 to 3 is the heat added, and the area under the line from 4 to 1 is the heat rejected. What is left of the first when the second is taken away is the area the cycle encloses, which is the net work, so the efficiency is the share of the whole area that the work area makes up.

That share depends on two temperatures. Heat enters over a range, from the cold water arriving at the boiler to the hot steam leaving it, and its **average heat-input temperature**, written $\bar T_{in}$, is the single temperature at which the *same* heat would have to enter to fill the same area. Heat leaves at the condenser temperature $T_c$. Because the pump and turbine are isentropic, states 1 and 2 share an entropy and so do 3 and 4, which makes both areas equally wide, and $q_{out} / q_{in} = T_c / \bar T_{in}$. The efficiency is therefore $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$. For the cycle you worked, $q_{out} / q_{in} = 2032.8 / 3218.0 = 0.632$, so with the condenser at 313 K its average heat-input temperature is 313 / 0.632 = 495 K, about 222 °C.

afterFigure.text: This is [[Carnot's expression|The greatest efficiency of an engine between two temperatures, 1 minus the cold temperature over the hot one, in kelvin. Met in 'Testing a claimed efficiency'.]] with an average in place of a single hot temperature, and it leaves only two ways to improve a cycle: raise $\bar T_{in}$ or lower $T_c$. The condenser cannot be colder than its cooling water allows, so the improvements a designer controls act mainly on $\bar T_{in}$. A condenser that cools its condensate below the saturation temperature also loses efficiency, because the extra heat removed has to be put back in the boiler, and the DOE handbook notes that operators can change a plant's efficiency directly through how warm the cooling water is and how fast it flows.

diagram.alt: A temperature-entropy diagram of a steam cycle. The area under the heating path is the heat added, the grey rectangle below the condenser line is the heat rejected, and the area left over is the net work. A dashed line marks the average heat-input temperature. In the second view the condenser is warmer, so the grey rectangle is taller and the net work area is smaller.
diagram.caption: The efficiency is the net work area as a share of the whole area. A warmer condenser takes work area away. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The cold side is set by the cooling water, so a plant can only watch it move with the seasons. The changes a designer controls act on the heat-input side.

lead.text: Raising the average heat-input temperature runs into a practical limit, which the first view of the figure shows. If the boiler delivers saturated steam, state 3 lies on the edge of the wet region and the expansion that follows ends well inside it, with a good share of the steam back as droplets. The droplets strike the blades at high speed and cause pitting and erosion, which wear the blades away and lower the turbine's efficiency.

The simplest remedy is **superheating**, which means heating the steam beyond saturation before it enters the turbine. State 3 then moves up and to the right, so the exhaust is drier, and the extra heat enters at the highest temperature in the cycle, which raises $\bar T_{in}$ as well. **Reheating** goes a step further: after the steam has expanded part of the way it returns to the boiler, is heated again to a temperature close to the first inlet temperature, and passes through a second turbine at lower pressure. Its purpose is to take out the moisture that the steam carries into the last stages of its expansion, and it raises the efficiency too, because more of the heat enters at a high temperature.

afterFigure.text: Reheating was tried in the 1920s and did not run for long because of technical difficulties, and it returned in the 1940s as high-pressure boilers became common. Most supercritical power plants today take steam at 24.1 MPa and 538 to 566 °C, which gives a plant efficiency of 40%, and raising the pressure to 31 MPa and the temperature to 600 °C reaches 42%.

diagram.alt: Three temperature-entropy diagrams of a steam cycle. With saturated steam at the turbine inlet the expansion ends deep inside the wet region. With superheated steam the path starts further right and the exhaust is drier, and the average heat-input temperature line is higher. With reheat the steam is returned to the heater part way down and the exhaust is drier still.
diagram.caption: Each change moves the average heat-input temperature up and the exhaust to the right, towards dry steam. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Reheating applies the same remedy part way down the turbine. The next screen turns to the cold end of the heating path, where a third change works.

lead.text: **Regeneration** works on the cold end of the heating path. Without it the boiler has to warm the feedwater all the way up from the condenser temperature, and heat added at those low temperatures drags the average heat-input temperature down. In a regenerative cycle some steam is tapped from the turbine part of the way through its expansion and sent to feedwater heaters, which warm the water between the condenser and the boiler. The boiler then starts from hotter feedwater, and more of the heat it adds enters at a high temperature, so the efficiency rises.

Tapping steam has a price, because the bled steam no longer expands through the rest of the turbine and gives up less work. The boiler has to add less heat as well, and the cycle's efficiency still rises, which is why regenerative cycles with feedwater heaters are commonly used in real power stations.

reveal.text: In the handbook's plant the reheated steam is at about 227 °C and the condenser holds about 6.9 kPa. Every stage you ordered is a Rankine process: expansion, heating, expansion, heat removal and pumping.

lessons.orientation: Trace the Rankine cycle through pump, boiler, turbine and condenser, compute its efficiency from state enthalpies, and decide which change raises it and why.
lessons.reviewLabel: Reading and improving a steam cycle
lessons.nextAction: Compute the ideal efficiency of a gas turbine from its pressure ratio, and say why real machines stop at pressure ratios of 11 to 16.

blocks.text: The cloud above a steam power station is not the steam that turned the turbine. That steam stays inside the plant, running round a closed loop from boiler to turbine to condenser and back through a pump, while the cloud comes from the cooling system that carries away the condenser's heat. A plant that runs on a single steam cycle is limited to an efficiency of 35 to 42%, so well over half of the heat it takes in leaves through that condenser.

Why must a plant that works so hard to make hot steam give most of the heat away, and which changes to the loop would let it give away a little less? Four numbers read at the corners of the loop are enough to answer both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out a steam cycle's efficiency from four state enthalpies and say which change to the plant would raise it, and why.
intro.whyItMatters: Whatever heats the boiler, a steam plant is a Rankine loop, so the same four numbers let you judge any of them.

recap.keyIdea: A steam cycle's efficiency is its net work divided by the heat the boiler adds, and it rises when the heat enters at a higher average temperature or leaves at a lower one.

blocks.text: The four states of the Rankine loop give four balances: the pump takes $h_2 - h_1$, the boiler adds $h_3 - h_2$, the turbine delivers $h_3 - h_4$ and the condenser removes $h_4 - h_1$. The thermal efficiency is the net work over the heat added, a feed pump that takes 1 to 3% of the turbine's output is normal, and a share far outside that range points to an error in the data.

For the ideal cycle $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$, so a warmer condenser lowers the efficiency, while superheating, reheating and regeneration raise the average heat-input temperature. Superheating and reheating also dry the exhaust, which spares the last blades from droplets.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson swaps the steam for hot air and asks why a gas turbine's ideal efficiency depends on its pressure ratio and not on how hot it burns.

lessons.title: Gas turbines and the pressure ratio

lead.text: A gas turbine has three components. The compressor takes in air from the atmosphere and raises its pressure, from state 1 to state 2, the combustor burns fuel in the compressed air at roughly constant pressure, from 2 to 3, and the hot gas expands through the turbine, from 3 to 4, and leaves as exhaust. The cycle that describes this is the **Brayton cycle**. Because the air comes from the atmosphere and the exhaust goes back to it, the real machine is an *open* cycle, although it is analysed as if the exhaust were reused and the loop closed.

In the ideal cycle the compression and the expansion are isentropic, so they are vertical lines on a temperature-entropy diagram, while heat is added and rejected at constant pressure. The turbine does more work than the compressor takes, because the gas entering it has been heated, and part of the turbine's work drives the compressor through the shaft. Only what remains is the output.

diagram.alt: A gas turbine drawn as a compressor, a combustor and a turbine on one shaft with a load. Air enters the compressor, fuel is burned in the combustor, and the hot gas expands through the turbine. The second view draws the ideal cycle on a temperature-entropy diagram, with compression and expansion as vertical lines.
diagram.caption: Air goes through three components and leaves as hot exhaust. Use the buttons to see the ideal cycle on a T-s diagram.

lead.text: For the ideal Brayton cycle the efficiency is $\eta = 1 - r_p^{-(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}$, where $r_p$ is the pressure ratio, the pressure leaving the compressor divided by the pressure entering it, and $\gamma$ is the heat capacity ratio of the gas. For air $\gamma$ is 1.4, which makes the exponent $0.4 / 1.4 = 0.286$, and the figure shows what follows: 44.8% at a ratio of 8, 50.8% at 12, 54.7% at 16 and 62.2% at 30.

Two things stand out. The curve keeps climbing, so the formula alone gives no reason to stop at any ratio, but it flattens, since going from 8 to 16 adds 9.9 points while doubling again to 32 adds only about 8. The formula also has **no temperature in it**. The turbine's *firing temperature*, which runs from 900 to 1,400 °C in open-circuit machines, does not change the ideal efficiency, and it changes how much power each kilogram of air produces.

steps.headline: Find the ideal efficiency of a gas turbine with a pressure ratio of 16, taking $\gamma = 1.4$.

workedSteps.text: The pressure ratio is raised to a power that depends on the gas. Choose the exponent.
Raise 16 to that power, using logarithms.
The efficiency is one minus the reciprocal of that number.
The curve in the figure gives the same value. It is an upper limit, because a real machine has losses that the ideal cycle leaves out.

reveal.text: What the hotter inlet changes is the power from each kilogram of air. A real machine does gain efficiency from a hotter inlet, and the limit is whether the first stage of turbine blades survives it, but that gain comes from effects the ideal formula leaves out.

lead.text: The formula would have designers raise the ratio without limit, and the first obstacle is temperature. The compressor heats the air as it compresses it, so a higher ratio delivers hotter air to the combustor. The turbine's inlet temperature has a limit set by the metal and the life required of it, so the hotter the air arrives, the smaller the temperature rise left for burning fuel. In the figure the limit is drawn at 1,400 °C, the top of the firing range, with air entering at 300 K. The compressor outlet is 543 K at a ratio of 8, 662 K at 16 and 793 K at 30, and the room left for fuel heat shrinks from about 1,130 K to 1,010 K to 880 K.

Two further reasons point the same way. In the high-pressure stages the compressor blades are short, so the running gap between blade tips and casing is a larger share of the blade height and more air leaks past the tips, which lowers the compressor's efficiency, most of all in small turbines. And because the efficiency curve levels off, little is gained by raising a ratio that is already high. Together these hold most common designs to a ratio of about 11 to 16, where the ideal efficiency is already 49.6 to 54.7%. The largest modern machines run higher ratios: Wikipedia's article on combined cycles gives the General Electric 9HA, the turbine in the plant certified in 2016 as the world's most efficient combined-cycle plant, an overall pressure ratio of 21.8 to 1.

As the pressure ratio rises from 8 to 16 to 30, the air leaves the compressor hotter, at 543, 662 and 793 kelvin, and the temperature range left under the limit for burning fuel shrinks from about 1,130 to 1,010 to 880 kelvin.

reveal.text: The ideal curve says nothing about materials, which is why the real limit sits where the turbine metal and the compressor blades put it.

lead.text: A gas turbine's exhaust leaves hot, and a **recuperator** is a heat exchanger that uses it to preheat the compressed air before it reaches the combustor, so that less fuel has to be burned to reach the same turbine inlet temperature. It works only when the exhaust is hotter than the compressed air, and that depends on the pressure ratio. A low ratio with a large temperature rise in the combustor leaves the exhaust well above the compressed air, and a high ratio does the reverse.

In the ideal cycle with 300 K air and a 1,400 °C turbine inlet, the exhaust at a ratio of 4 leaves at 1,126 K while the compressed air is at 446 K, which leaves 680 K to use. At 16 the difference is down to 95 K, and at 30 the compressed air, at 793 K, is hotter than the exhaust at 633 K, so the heat would have to flow the wrong way. Heat recycling of this kind is therefore possible only in an engine that runs at a low pressure ratio in the first place, a low-efficiency mode. Moving heat from the exhaust to the air entering the compressor would make things worse, because hotter inlet air takes more work to compress.

diagram.alt: Three pairs of bars comparing the temperature of the air leaving the compressor with the temperature of the turbine exhaust. At a pressure ratio of 4 the exhaust, 1,126 kelvin, is much hotter than the compressed air, 446 kelvin. At 16 the exhaust is only 95 kelvin hotter. At 30 the compressed air, 793 kelvin, is hotter than the exhaust, 633 kelvin.
diagram.caption: A recuperator can only move heat from exhaust to compressed air while the exhaust is the hotter of the two. Use the buttons to raise the pressure ratio.

lessons.orientation: Compute the ideal Brayton efficiency from the pressure ratio, explain why real machines stop at pressure ratios of 11 to 16, and say when a recuperator pays.
lessons.reviewLabel: Gas turbines and the pressure ratio
lessons.nextAction: Use the ideal Otto and Diesel formulas to compare petrol and diesel engines, and say what limits the compression ratio of each.

blocks.text: A gas turbine draws in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and expands the hot gas through a turbine, whose work drives both the compressor and the generator. The ideal efficiency of that loop depends on a single number, the pressure ratio of the compressor, and it keeps rising as the ratio does: with $\gamma = 1.4$ the formula gives 50.8% at a ratio of 12 and 62.2% at a ratio of 30.

Yet gas turbines of the most common designs have pressure ratios of about 11 to 16, and large machines in simple cycle are quoted at around 41.5 to 43%, well below even the ideal value for 12. Why do designers stop where they do, and why is the real figure so far under the ideal one?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute an ideal gas-turbine efficiency from its pressure ratio, explain why designers stop at ratios of 11 to 16, and decide when a recuperator pays.
intro.whyItMatters: Gas turbines power jet engines and many new power stations, and the pressure ratio is the first number to check on any of them.

recap.keyIdea: The ideal efficiency of a gas turbine depends only on its pressure ratio and gamma, real designs stop at 11 to 16 because hot compressor air leaves little room under the metal limit, and a recuperator pays only while the exhaust is hotter than the compressed air.

blocks.text: The ideal Brayton efficiency is $1 - r_p^{-(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}$, which for air gives 50.8% at a ratio of 12 and 62.2% at 30. The firing temperature does not appear in it, although a hotter turbine inlet raises the power of each kilogram of air, and part of the turbine's work always drives the compressor.

A higher ratio delivers hotter air from the compressor, which leaves less temperature rise before the turbine's metal limit, and the curve flattens, so most common designs sit at 11 to 16. A recuperator can use the exhaust to preheat the compressed air only while the exhaust is the hotter stream, which means at a low ratio. Real simple-cycle machines come out at around 41.5 to 43%, because compression and expansion are not isentropic.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to petrol and diesel engines, where the compression ratio plays the part of the pressure ratio and a different limit, knock, stops it.

lessons.title: Petrol and diesel engines

lead.text: The **Otto cycle** idealises a typical spark-ignition engine, the kind found in most cars, and is named after Nicolaus Otto. In one cycle the gas is compressed isentropically, from state 1 to 2. Heat is added at constant volume, from 2 to 3, as the fuel burns. The gas then expands isentropically, from 3 to 4, and delivers the work, and heat is rejected at constant volume, from 4 to 1, when the exhaust is let go. The ratio of the cylinder's largest volume to its smallest, $r = V_1 / V_2$, is the **compression ratio**.

Working through the four processes with the ideal-gas relations gives the ideal efficiency $\eta = 1 - 1 / r^{\gamma - 1}$, which contains only the compression ratio and $\gamma$, the heat capacity ratio of the gas. Because $\gamma$ is 1.4 for air, a larger $r$ always gives a larger $\eta$, so on paper the way to a better engine is to compress harder.

diagram.alt: A pressure-volume diagram of the ideal Otto cycle on logarithmic axes. The gas is compressed from state 1 to 2, heat is added at constant volume from 2 to 3 so the pressure jumps, the gas expands from 3 to 4 and heat is rejected at constant volume from 4 to 1.
diagram.caption: Compression, a jump in pressure at constant volume, expansion, and a drop at constant volume, on logarithmic axes.
