steps.headline: Find the ideal efficiency of an Otto engine with a compression ratio of 9, taking $\gamma = 1.4$.

workedSteps.text: The exponent is $\gamma - 1$, because the compression ratio compares volumes.
Raise the compression ratio to that power.
The efficiency is one minus the reciprocal.
The ideal efficiency is 58.5%. A real engine falls well short of it, because heat and friction losses are left out of the formula.

reveal.text: Each added unit of compression ratio buys less than the one before. The next screen shows the whole curve, and what happens to it when the gas changes.

lead.text: The formula gives a family of curves, because $\gamma$ is not the same everywhere in the cylinder. For air it is 1.4, and the first curve in the figure reaches 60.2% at a compression ratio of 10, which is about what the standard car engine uses. The combustion products of the fuel and air mixture, however, have a $\gamma$ of about 1.3, and with that value the same ratio of 10 gives 49.9% and the whole curve drops.

A change in the assumed gas therefore moves the answer by ten points while the engine stays the same. That is the sense in which these are *ideal* figures: they are upper limits worked out for a model gas, with no heat loss or friction in them, and the thermal efficiency of an actual engine is significantly lower.

diagram.alt: A graph of ideal Otto efficiency against compression ratio from 2 to 20. With gamma 1.4 for air the curve reaches 60.2 percent at a ratio of 10. With gamma 1.3 for combustion products it reaches 49.9 percent at the same ratio. A dashed line marks the typical petrol engine ratio of about 10.
diagram.caption: Both curves rise with the compression ratio, but the gas model moves the whole curve. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The next screen turns to the reason a petrol engine stays near the ratio of 10 that the figure marks.

lead.text: If a higher compression ratio always gives a higher ideal efficiency, a petrol engine might as well run at 20, where the formula gives 69.8%. The standard ratio for a typical car is about 10:1 instead, and it does not rise much, because of what compression does to the mixture. The harder the fuel and air are compressed, the hotter they get, and if the mixture becomes too hot before the flame front reaches it, it ignites by itself before the compression stroke is finished. This self-ignition is called **knock**.

Knock can damage engine components and it decreases the engine's power, and at a high ratio it would severely reduce the efficiency as well. It therefore sets a ceiling on the compression ratio of a petrol engine, which the formula, with its steady rise, cannot show.

reveal.text: The limit comes from the fuel and not from the cycle, which suggests an engine that does not give the fuel a chance to ignite early.

lead.text: A diesel engine avoids knock by compressing air alone. The fuel is injected into the compressed air only when the compression is nearly finished, and it ignites from the heat that the compression generated, so no spark plug is needed. Self-ignition, a fault in a petrol engine, is the behaviour a diesel relies on, and no fuel is in the cylinder to ignite early.

The fuel burns as it is injected, so heat is added at about constant pressure while the piston moves out a little. The ideal efficiency of this **Diesel cycle** depends on the compression ratio and on the **cut-off ratio** $\alpha = V_3 / V_2$, the volume at the end of the burn divided by the volume at its start: $\eta = 1 - \frac{1}{r^{\gamma - 1}} \cdot \frac{\alpha^{\gamma} - 1}{\gamma (\alpha - 1)}$. The second factor is always greater than 1, so at the same ratio the ideal Otto cycle is the more efficient. With an illustrative cut-off ratio of 2 and a ratio of 10, Otto gives 60.2% and Diesel gives 53.4%.

afterFigure.text: The diesel's advantage is the ratio it can use. With no mixture to knock, a diesel runs at a much higher compression ratio, and at 20 the same formula gives 64.7%, above the petrol engine at 10. A real diesel is more efficient overall for this reason, and the Otto formula also leaves out the throttling losses that a diesel does not have.

diagram.alt: Three pressure-volume diagrams. The Otto cycle at compression ratio 10 has ideal efficiency 60.2 percent. The Diesel cycle at the same ratio, with a cut-off ratio of 2 so that heat is added at constant pressure, has 53.4 percent. The Diesel cycle at ratio 20 has 64.7 percent, higher than the Otto cycle at 10.

reveal.text: Very large marine diesels burn 0.16 kg of fuel per kilowatt-hour, which is less than any other large engine that runs on a single cycle.

lead.text: Both devices push more air into the cylinders, which raises the power an engine of a given size can deliver, but they take their energy from different places. A **turbocharger** uses a turbine in the exhaust stream to remove part of the energy that would otherwise leave with the exhaust and to transfer it to the intake air. Because that energy was being wasted, the engine's efficiency can rise as well as its power.

A **supercharger** is driven by the crankshaft. It raises the power output without raising the efficiency, because it spends some of the engine's net work to pressurise the intake air and recovers none of the wasted exhaust energy. Compressing air also heats it, and in a petrol engine the intake air has to be cooled again in an intercooler, which also makes it denser, so that premature ignition is avoided and more mass enters each cylinder.

reveal.text: A turbocharger changes the energy balance because it uses energy that was leaving anyway. The next question combines it with knock.
Boosting and knock meet at the intake: the more the air is compressed, the more heat has to be taken out of it before it reaches the cylinder.

lessons.orientation: Use the ideal Otto and Diesel efficiency formulas to compare the engines, explain why compression ratio is limited in one and not the other, and judge claims about turbochargers and superchargers.
lessons.nextAction: Combine the efficiencies of a gas-turbine topping cycle and a steam bottoming cycle, and say what a combined heat and power figure does and does not tell you.

blocks.text: Very large marine diesels burn 0.16 kg of fuel per kilowatt-hour, a lower specific fuel consumption than any other large engine that runs on a single cycle. Yet the ideal formulas say that, at the same compression ratio, the ideal petrol cycle is more efficient than the ideal cycle of a diesel.

Both statements hold, and the way to see it is to ask what limits the compression ratio of each engine. The formula for the petrol engine is the place to start, since the compression ratio and the gas in the cylinder are the only things in it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute the ideal efficiency of a petrol engine, explain why knock caps its compression ratio and diesels avoid it, and judge claims about turbochargers and superchargers.
intro.whyItMatters: The compression ratio is the main design choice in a piston engine, and these formulas show what it can buy and what stops it.

recap.keyIdea: The ideal Otto efficiency rises with the compression ratio, knock caps a petrol engine near 10:1, and a diesel compresses air alone, which lets it use a higher ratio.

blocks.text: The ideal efficiency of an Otto engine is $1 - 1 / r^{\gamma - 1}$, which gives 58.5% at a ratio of 9 and 60.2% at 10 for air, and 49.9% at 10 when $\gamma$ is taken as 1.3. Ideal values are upper limits that depend on the gas model, and real engines come out significantly lower because of heat and friction losses.

Knock, the self-ignition of a hot compressed mixture, holds a petrol engine to about 10:1. A diesel compresses air alone and relies on self-ignition, so it runs a higher ratio, and although the ideal Otto cycle is better at equal ratios, a real diesel is more efficient overall. A turbocharger recovers exhaust energy and can add efficiency, while a crankshaft-driven supercharger adds power only.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson stacks two cycles on one supply of fuel and asks how their efficiencies combine.

lessons.title: Stacking cycles and using the waste heat

lead.text: In a combined-cycle plant the working fluid of the first engine, after completing its cycle, is still hot enough for a second engine to extract energy from it. The first engine, usually a gas turbine running the [[Brayton cycle|The ideal gas-turbine cycle of compressor, combustor and turbine. Met in 'Gas turbines and the pressure ratio'.]], is the **topping cycle**, and the second, usually a steam plant running the [[Rankine cycle|The ideal steam loop of pump, boiler, turbine and condenser. Met in 'Reading and improving a steam cycle'.]], is the **bottoming cycle**. A heat exchanger sits between them, which lets the two engines use different working fluids, and in a heat-recovery steam generator the flue gas at 450 to 650 °C raises steam at a temperature between 420 and 580 °C.

Steam suits the second place because of the temperatures. A gas turbine's firing temperature is 900 to 1,400 °C, while a steam plant needs expensive alloys for its hottest parts and is held to about 655 °C, and the water that cools its condenser can be as cold as 15 °C. That low steam entry temperature, compared with a gas turbine's, is the reason steam is the usual bottoming cycle, and with the two engines together the plant as a whole works across the range from the gas turbine's firing temperature down to the cold of the condenser.

reveal.text: Each engine uses the heat left by the one above it. The next screen turns that into a rule for combining their efficiencies.

lead.text: Suppose the gas turbine converts 43% of the fuel's energy into work. The other 57% leaves as hot exhaust, and that is all the bottoming cycle has to work with, because it burns no fuel of its own. If the steam cycle converts a fraction $\eta_b$ of what it receives, the plant's overall efficiency is $\eta = \eta_t + (1 - \eta_t)\,\eta_b$, where $\eta_t$ is the topping cycle's efficiency.

A plant that reaches 64% from a gas turbine of 43% must therefore have a steam cycle that converts $(0.64 - 0.43) / 0.57 = 0.368$ of the exhaust heat, or 36.8%. That lies inside the 35 to 42% of a steam plant running alone, so the figures agree, and the 21 points that the steam cycle adds are its share of the *fuel* energy, which is why they are a fraction of the 57 and not of the 100.

diagram.alt: A bar for 100 units of fuel energy. With a gas turbine alone, 43 units become work and 57 leave in the exhaust. In the combined cycle, 43 units become gas-turbine work, the steam cycle converts 21 of the 57 exhaust units into work, and 36 are lost, so the overall efficiency is 64 percent and the steam cycle's own efficiency is 21 over 57, or 36.8 percent.

steps.headline: Find the overall efficiency of a plant whose gas turbine converts 38% of the fuel energy and whose steam cycle converts 35% of the exhaust heat.

workedSteps.text: The steam cycle works only on the energy the gas turbine left.
It converts 35% of that.
The plant's efficiency is the gas turbine's share plus the steam cycle's.
At 59.7% the plant is a little above the 55 to 59% that most large units reach at their peak on the lower heating value, so the figures are believable for a good plant.

reveal.text: Wording like this is common in summaries, and the safe habit is to rebuild the figure from what each cycle receives.

lead.text: Two plants can burn the same fuel and quote different efficiencies, because the fuel's energy can be counted in two ways. The **higher heating value**, HHV, includes the latent heat of vaporisation of the water formed in combustion, which a condensing boiler could recover. The **lower heating value**, LHV, leaves it out. For methane the HHV is 55.50 MJ/kg and the LHV is 50.00 MJ/kg, a difference of 11%.

The same electricity divided by a smaller fuel energy gives a larger number, so an efficiency quoted on the LHV always reads higher than the same plant's on the HHV. For methane $\eta_{HHV} = \eta_{LHV} \times 50.00 / 55.50 = 0.901\,\eta_{LHV}$. The Baglan Bay power station reached nearly 60% on the LHV, which is 54% on the HHV, and the figure converts four invented plant claims to both bases. Other fuels have other ratios, so the factor 0.901 belongs to methane.

The second view fills in each plant's figure on both bases: A is 54.1 percent on the higher basis, B is 62.2 percent on the lower, C is 52.3 higher and D is 57.7 lower.

steps.headline: A combined-cycle plant burning methane is quoted at 56% on the lower heating value. Find its efficiency on the higher heating value.

workedSteps.text: The same electricity is divided by a larger fuel energy on the HHV basis, so the HHV figure will be the smaller one.
Choose the factor that converts the LHV figure to the HHV figure.
Multiply the quoted figure by that factor.
The quoted figure flatters the plant by about 5.5 points, and the gap is about 11% of the LHV figure.

lead.text: A power plant rejects most of the energy it does not convert as low-temperature heat, and **combined heat and power**, also called cogeneration, sells that heat for industrial processes or district heating instead of discarding it. Where winters are cold, selling hot water from a power plant for heating is common, and such systems can yield theoretical efficiencies above 95%.

A figure like that is a *total*, which adds electricity and useful heat, two different forms of energy. Take an invented plant that sends out 35 units of electricity and 55 units of heat for every 100 units of fuel. Its total is 90% and its electrical efficiency is still 35%. The total says how much of the fuel energy found a use, and it says nothing about how much became electricity. A combined-cycle plant at 60% gives more electricity from the same fuel, 60 units against 35, while the CHP plant gives more useful energy, 90 units against 60, but only if someone uses all of its heat.

diagram.alt: Two bars for 100 units of fuel energy. A combined-cycle power plant turns 60 into electricity and loses 40. An invented CHP plant sends out 35 units of electricity and 55 units of heat and loses 10, so its total efficiency is 90 percent but its electrical efficiency is 35 percent.

reveal.text: A total efficiency is a fair figure for a CHP plant when it says what it counts. The trouble starts when it is read as an electrical efficiency.

lead.text: The 64% in a brochure is a best case. A combined-cycle efficiency of over 60% belongs to a plant that is new, unaged and running at continuous output, and most units, especially the larger ones, reach peak steady-state efficiencies of 55 to 59% on the lower heating value. Efficiency falls whenever the plant is not running at continuous output. A gas turbine can often start quickly and gives power at once, but the steam cycle takes time to warm up, and until it is running the efficiency is much lower, which can take an hour or more.

reveal.text: A figure for a plant has to be read with its fuel basis, what it counts, and how the plant is run. The checks at the end of the lesson use all three.

lessons.orientation: Combine the efficiencies of a gas-turbine topping cycle and a steam bottoming cycle, compare efficiencies stated on different fuel bases, and say what a combined heat and power figure does and does not tell you.
lessons.reviewLabel: Stacking cycles and using the waste heat
lessons.nextAction: Name the four components of a vapour-compression machine, compute COP for cooling and heating, and judge a quoted COP against the Carnot limit.

blocks.text: A gas turbine on its own converts, say, 43% of the energy in its fuel into work, and its exhaust leaves at 450 to 650 °C. A combined-cycle plant that uses that exhaust to raise steam for a second engine reaches as much as 64%, while a steam plant working alone is limited to 35 to 42%.

The figures invite a quick sum: 43% from the gas turbine plus 37% from a steam plant would make 80%, and the plant reaches 64%. Where did the other 16 points go, and what does that say about how efficiencies combine?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to stack the efficiencies of two cycles correctly, compare efficiencies quoted on different fuel bases, and say what a combined heat and power figure does and does not tell you.
intro.whyItMatters: Brochures quote efficiencies on different bases and count different things, and a fair comparison takes a few lines of arithmetic.

recap.keyIdea: In a combined cycle the second engine converts only what the first one left, so efficiencies stack and never add, and a quoted figure has to be read with its fuel basis, what it counts and how the plant runs.

blocks.text: With a gas turbine at 43% and a steam cycle that converts 36.8% of what is left, the plant reaches 64%, because $\eta = \eta_t + (1 - \eta_t)\,\eta_b$. Steam is the bottoming cycle because it can use heat at 420 to 580 °C, far below a gas turbine's firing temperature, and its condenser can be cooled to as low as 15 °C.

Quoted efficiencies need three checks. For methane a figure on the lower heating value reads about 11% higher than the same plant's on the higher heating value. A combined heat and power total counts the heat as well as the electricity. And the best figures belong to a new plant at continuous output, with lower values at start-up and at part load.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson runs an engine in reverse: heat pumps and refrigerators use work to move heat, and a quoted figure for them has to be checked against the Carnot limit.

lessons.title: Moving heat with work

lead.text: A heat pump, a refrigerator and an air conditioner are built from the same four parts: a compressor, a condenser, an expansion valve that works as a throttle, and an evaporator. The refrigerant circulates through them in a loop. It enters the compressor as a saturated vapour and leaves at a higher pressure and temperature as a superheated vapour. In the condenser it gives up heat to the air or water around it and condenses into a liquid, and the liquid then passes through the expansion valve, where its pressure drops abruptly and part of it flashes to vapour, which cools the mixture below the temperature of the space to be cooled. In the evaporator the cold mixture takes heat from that space and evaporates, and the vapour returns to the compressor.

The valve does no work and exchanges no heat, so the refrigerant leaves it with the enthalpy it came in with, which makes the flash evaporation [[isenthalpic|At constant enthalpy, as in an ideal throttling valve. Met in 'The energy balance on a device'.]]. Only the compressor takes work, $W$. Heat $Q_C$ enters at the evaporator from the cold space, and heat $Q_H$ leaves at the condenser into the warm one, so that by the first law $Q_H = Q_C + W$.

diagram.alt: A loop of four components: a compressor that takes work, a condenser that gives heat to the warm space, an expansion valve, and an evaporator that takes heat from the cold space. The second view shows the energy balance of one heat pump: 3.0 kilowatts from outdoors plus 1.0 kilowatt of work leave the condenser as 4.0 kilowatts, so the heating COP is 4.0 and the cooling COP is 3.0.
diagram.caption: Refrigerant circulates through four components. Heat is moved from the cold space to the warm one, and the work is added to it on the way. Use the buttons to see the balance.

reveal.text: The heat released is always larger than the heat taken in, by exactly the compressor's work. That surplus is what separates a heat pump's output from the heat it moves.

lead.text: The **coefficient of performance**, COP, compares the useful heating or cooling that a machine provides with the work it needs. It differs from an efficiency because its numerator is the heat *moved*. A refrigerator or air conditioner is judged by the heat it removes from the cold space, $COP_{cooling} = Q_C / W$, and a heat pump by the heat it delivers to the warm one, $COP_{heating} = Q_H / W$.

Because $Q_H = Q_C + W$, the heating COP is $(Q_C + W) / W = COP_{cooling} + 1$, so a machine's heating COP is exactly one larger than its cooling COP. A COP above 1 is normal, because the machine moves heat that already exists and the work only has to raise it from cold to warm, while an electrical resistance heater, which makes its heat from the electricity, has a COP of 1 or less. The COP also depends strongly on operating conditions, above all on the temperatures of the source and the sink, so a machine does not have one COP.

steps.headline: A refrigerator removes 2.4 kW from its cabinet using 0.8 kW of electricity. Find its cooling COP, its heat output and its heating COP.

workedSteps.text: The cooling COP is the heat removed over the work.
The condenser releases the heat taken in plus the work, as the first law requires.
Used as a heat pump, the same machine is judged by the heat it delivers.
The heating COP, 4.0, is exactly 1 more than the cooling COP, 3.0.

reveal.text: A resistance heater given the same 2.0 kW would deliver 2.0 kW. The heat pump delivers 7.0 kW, and the extra 5.0 kW is the heat it moved.
The conservation of energy is not in doubt: every kilowatt delivered is accounted for. What a COP above 1 shows is that the machine moves heat, which the work then has to raise from cold to warm.

lead.text: A heat pump is a heat engine run backwards, so its best possible COP is the reciprocal of the ideal engine's [[Carnot efficiency|The greatest efficiency of an engine between two temperatures, 1 minus the cold temperature over the hot, in kelvin. Met in 'Testing a claimed efficiency'.]]. Between a cold source at $T_C$ and a warm sink at $T_H$, both absolute, the limits are $COP_{heating} = T_H / (T_H - T_C)$ and $COP_{cooling} = T_C / (T_H - T_C)$. The standard European test for ground-source heat pump units puts the warm side at 308 K (35 °C) and the cold side at 273 K (0 °C), which gives limits of 308 / 35 = 8.8 for heating and 273 / 35 = 7.8 for cooling.

Real machines fall well below these limits. The best systems test at around 4.5, and when installed units are measured over a whole season, allowing for the energy to pump water through the pipes, seasonal heating COPs are around 3.5 or less. The temperatures must be absolute, because putting Celsius values into the formula gives nonsense: with a source at 0 °C, $35 / (35 - 0) = 1$ would rate a heat pump no better than a resistance heater.

reveal.text: The same pump delivering 35 °C had a limit of 8.8, so the hotter delivery has already cost 1.7 points of the ceiling.

lead.text: The figure plots measured COPs against the delivery temperature, with the Carnot limit for the same source drawn above them. For a high-efficiency air-source heat pump with air at 0 °C, the real machine reaches 3.8 against a limit of 8.8 when it delivers 35 °C, and 2.0 against 5.2 when it delivers 65 °C. Both lines fall as the delivery temperature rises, because the **lift**, the difference between the delivery temperature and the source temperature, grows, and the COP falls with it. A colder source has the same effect: with air at -20 °C the limit is 5.6 at 35 °C and the real machine reaches 2.2.

A source at 270 K delivering to a building at 280 K, a lift of 10 K, has a Carnot COP of 28, and heating the building to 300 K, a lift of 30 K, brings it down to 10. Heat pumps therefore perform best in moderate climates and lose efficiency as outdoor temperatures drop. A ground source, whose temperature stays nearly constant, is spared the large swings, which makes it the most efficient kind of heat pump.

afterFigure.text: The delivery temperature depends on what the heat is for: a heated floor can run at 35 °C, while radiators and hot water need 55 °C and more. The same machine therefore has several COPs, one for each job.

diagram.alt: Graphs of heat-pump COP against delivery temperature from 35 to 85 degrees Celsius. With air at 0 degrees the Carnot limit falls from 8.8 to 4.2 and the real unit from 3.8 to 2.0. With air at minus 20 degrees the limit is 5.6 at 35 degrees and the real unit 2.2. For a ground source at 10 degrees they are 12.3 and 7.2. Every line falls as the delivery temperature rises.

lessons.orientation: Name the four components of a vapour-compression machine, compute COP for cooling and heating, and judge a quoted COP against the Carnot limit at the stated temperatures.
lessons.nextAction: Build a series resistance network for a wall or pipe, find which resistance controls the heat flow, and decide whether more insulation helps.

blocks.text: An electric resistance heater turns each kilowatt-hour of electricity into one kilowatt-hour of heat and no more. A well-designed heat pump in mild weather delivers three to five kilowatt-hours of heat for every kilowatt-hour of electricity it uses.

That can look like a breach of the conservation of energy, since more energy comes out than goes in. Where does the extra heat come from, and why does a machine that is so much better in mild weather do worse when the weather turns cold?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to follow the heat through a vapour-compression machine, compute a coefficient of performance, and test a quoted COP against the Carnot limit at the stated temperatures.
intro.whyItMatters: Heat-pump brochures quote COPs freely, and the Carnot limit at the stated temperatures tells you which of them cannot be true.

recap.keyIdea: A heat pump moves heat with work, so its COP can exceed 1, its heating COP is its cooling COP plus 1, and the Carnot limit in kelvin caps any quoted COP, which falls as the lift grows.

blocks.text: A vapour-compression machine has four components: a compressor that takes the work, a condenser that releases heat, an expansion valve that throttles the refrigerant at constant enthalpy and an evaporator that absorbs heat. The first law gives $Q_H = Q_C + W$, so the heating COP is the cooling COP plus 1, and a COP above 1 breaks no law, because the machine moves heat that already exists.

The Carnot limit $T_H / (T_H - T_C)$, in kelvin, caps the COP at the stated temperatures, and real machines reach a fraction of it: 3.8 against 8.8 for an air-source unit delivering 35 °C from air at 0 °C. The COP falls as the lift grows, which happens with a hotter delivery temperature or a colder source.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from machines to walls and pipes, where heat flows through layers in series and the largest resistance decides how much.

lessons.title: Thermal resistance in series

lead.text: In steady conditions the same heat passes through every layer of a wall, because a layer whose temperature is not changing cannot store any. For a layer of thickness $\Delta x$ and conductivity $k$, [[Fourier's law|The heat flux through a layer is its conductivity times the temperature difference across it, divided by its thickness. Met in 'How heat moves' in Physics II.]] gives the heat flux as $q = k\,\Delta T / \Delta x$, and turning that round shows that the temperature difference needed to drive a given flux is $q\,\Delta x / k$. The quantity $\Delta x / k$ plays the part of a resistance, and it is called the layer's **thermal resistance**, written $R$ and measured in m²K/W.

The DOE handbook draws the comparison with electricity directly. Temperature difference plays the part of voltage, which gives the Fourier equation a form like Ohm's law, and heat flux plays the part of current. Layers in series then add their resistances as resistors do, so $q = \Delta T / (R_1 + R_2 + R_3)$.
Because one flux crosses every layer, layer $i$ takes a share of the total temperature difference equal to $q R_i$. The layers with the largest resistances take the largest drops.
A wall's layers are described by their resistances, and the inside is held 20 K above the outside.

reveal.text: The middle layer holds most of the resistance, so it also takes most of the temperature difference.

steps.headline: Find the heat flux through the copper, board and fibreglass wall, with 278 K across it.

lead.text: This is the handbook's composite wall, converted to SI units: 25.4 mm of copper with $k$ = 415 W/(m K), 3.2 mm of insulating board with $k$ = 0.083 W/(m K), and 50.8 mm of fibreglass with $k$ = 0.038 W/(m K).

workedSteps.text: Each layer's resistance is its thickness in metres divided by its conductivity. Copper first.
The board and the fibreglass follow in the same way.
The layers are in series, so the resistances add.
The flux is the temperature difference divided by the total resistance.
The handbook gets 64.2 Btu/(hr ft²) for this wall, which is 202 W/m² in SI units.

lead.text: The three resistances in the worked example are 0.000061, 0.0386 and 1.337 m²K/W, and they are very unequal. The fibreglass holds 97% of the total, the board 2.8%, and the copper plate, which is about eight times thicker than the board, less than 0.01%. A layer that holds most of the resistance is the **dominant resistance**, and it sets the heat flow.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows what that means in practice. Doubling the copper changes the total by less than 0.005%, which does not show in the flux at three figures, doubling the board lowers the flux by about 3%, and doubling the fibreglass nearly halves it. The temperature difference follows the same shares, with 270 K of the 278 K falling across the fibreglass. **Improving a layer pays in proportion to the share of the resistance it holds**, so the first step in any insulation decision is to find the layer that holds most of it.

diagram.alt: Four views of the wall's layer resistances as horizontal bars on one scale. In the as-built wall the fibreglass bar is by far the longest, 97 percent of the total, and the copper bar is too short to see. Doubling the copper changes nothing visible, doubling the board changes the total slightly, and doubling the fibreglass nearly doubles the total and halves the flux.
diagram.caption: Each bar is a layer's resistance, and the figure under it gives the total and the flux. Use the buttons to double one layer at a time.

lead.text: The same flux crosses all three layers of the wall.

reveal.text: The 270 K across the fibreglass and 7.8 K across the board add, with 0.01 K across the copper, to the 278 K applied to the wall.

lead.text: Where a surface meets a moving fluid, the heat has to cross a thin stagnant film of fluid, the **convection film**, before it reaches the bulk of the stream. The handbook writes the convective heat transfer as $Q = h A \Delta T$, so that per unit area $q = h\,\Delta T$, which has the form $q = \Delta T / R$ with $R = 1/h$. The film is therefore one more resistance in the series, and $h$ is the **convective heat transfer coefficient**. No single property of the fluid fixes $h$. The handbook treats it as measured and tabulated for each fluid and flow, and notes that turbulent flow has a higher $h$ than laminar flow because the stagnant film is thinner.

Whether the film matters depends on what else is in series with it. For the handbook's bare steam line, 6.7 m long and 457 mm across, with a surface at 138 °C in a room at 22 °C and $h$ = 102 W/(m² K) for the air, the surface temperature is given, so the film is the whole resistance and the loss is $h A \Delta T$, about 114 kW. Put 25.4 mm of insulation with $k$ = 1.38 W/(m K) on a wall whose film has $h$ = 5,400 W/(m² K), another of the handbook's cases, and the film's resistance is a hundredth of the total.

afterFigure.text: A film can be left out when a much larger resistance sits in series with it, and it has to be kept when it is the only resistance between the surface and the surroundings.

reveal.text: Insulation puts a new, large resistance in series with the film. The metal wall adds almost nothing, and blowing air makes the loss worse.

steps.headline: Pipes and the log mean area

lead.text: A flat layer has the same area at both faces, but a pipe wall does not: heat flows outward through a surface that grows with the radius, so the heat flux falls as it goes. The handbook points out that for a pipe wall neither the inner surface area nor the outer one is the right area to use. It defines the **log mean area**, $A_{lm} = (A_o - A_i) / \ln(A_o / A_i)$, which lies between the two, and with it the conduction equation for a cylindrical layer keeps its flat-wall form.

The second form follows when the areas are written as $2\pi r L$, and it is the easier one to use because only the ratio of the radii appears. Here $R$ is the resistance of a length $L$ of pipe in K/W, so a 1 m length of pipe has $R = \ln(r_o/r_i)/(2\pi k)$. The layers of a pipe add in series like those of a wall, each with its own radii and conductivity.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the handbook's pipe, converted to SI units: a steel wall 25.4 mm thick round a bore of 127 mm radius, covered with 76.2 mm of insulation. The two layers have different log mean areas, 0.875 m² and 1.181 m² per metre of pipe, and each is a little below the plain average of its inner and outer areas.

diagram.alt: Cross-section of a steel pipe covered with insulation, drawn to scale: bore 127 millimetres radius, steel out to 152.4, insulation out to 228.6. One view highlights the steel wall and one the insulation, each with its radii, conductivity and the inner, outer and log mean surface areas per metre of pipe.

steps.headline: Find the heat loss per metre of the handbook's pipe, with the inside wall 250 K hotter than the outside of the insulation.

lead.text: The steel has $k$ = 21.6 W/(m K) between radii of 127 mm and 152.4 mm, and the insulation has $k$ = 0.242 W/(m K) between 152.4 mm and 228.6 mm. All resistances are for one metre of pipe.

workedSteps.text: The steel wall comes first, from the logarithm form of the cylinder resistance.
The insulation uses the same form, with its own radii and its own conductivity. Work out its resistance.
The two resistances add, and the heat loss is the temperature difference divided by their sum.
The handbook gets 971 Btu/(hr ft) for this pipe, which is 934 W/m, the same result within rounding.

lead.text: Compare what each change does to the total resistance of the pipe.

reveal.text: The insulation holds 99.5% of the pipe's resistance, and 248.7 K of the 250 K falls across it.

lead.text: Putting insulation on a pipe adds a resistance, but it also gives the outside of the pipe a larger surface, and a larger surface lowers the film's resistance. On a large pipe the first effect wins at once. On a very thin cylinder the second can win for a while, so that the first layers of insulation raise the loss, and the outer radius at which the trend reverses is the **critical radius**. Wikipedia's article on thermal insulation states the consequence: below that radius, added insulation increases the heat transfer.

The critical radius depends only on the insulation's conductivity and the film coefficient. Taking the conductivity of the handbook's pipe insulation, $k$ = 0.242 W/(m K), and the film coefficient of its room air, $h$ = 102 W/(m² K), gives 2.37 mm. That pairing is a case made for this lesson, since the handbook gives no critical radius.

afterFigure.text: The figure compares a hypothetical bare wire of radius 0.5 mm with a bare tube of radius 5 mm. The wire loses more and more heat until the insulation reaches 2.4 mm, and is back to its bare loss only at about 55 mm. The tube is already beyond the critical radius, so every layer reduces its loss. A pipe with a radius well above 2.4 mm is already past it, so the thin wire is the case to watch.

diagram.alt: A graph of heat loss compared with the bare surface against the outer radius of the insulation, on a logarithmic axis. For a wire of radius 0.5 millimetres the loss rises to a peak of about 1.9 times the bare loss at 2.4 millimetres and falls back to the bare value near 55 millimetres. For a tube of radius 5 millimetres, already above the critical radius, the loss falls from the first layer.
diagram.caption: A hypothetical wire and tube in the handbook's room air, with insulation of conductivity 0.242 W/(m K). Use the buttons to compare a thin wire with a larger tube.

lead.text: Use the insulation and the air from the last screen.

reveal.text: A cylinder whose outer radius is already above the critical radius gains from every layer of insulation. A smaller one loses more heat until the insulation passes it.

lead.text: The usual expectation is that more insulation means less loss.

reveal.text: Compared with the bare wire's loss of 1, the wrapped wire loses about 1.8. Only insulation out to about 55 mm brings the loss back to what the bare wire lost.

blocks.text: A wall is built from 25.4 mm of copper plate, 3.2 mm of insulating board and 50.8 mm of fibreglass, and 278 K is held across it. The same heat passes through all three layers, so thickening any one of them would cut the loss, and the figure draws them to scale.

Copper is a thick metal plate, the board is the thinnest layer and the fibreglass the thickest, and the picture does not show which of them would do most for the money. The answer comes from giving each layer a number for how strongly it resists the heat and adding the numbers, in the way that resistors in series are added.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find which layer controls the heat flow through a wall or pipe, and when more insulation stops helping.
intro.whyItMatters: It shows where money spent on insulation or on a better pipe wall will make a difference.

recap.keyIdea: Layers and films in series add their resistances, the largest resistance controls the heat flow and takes most of the temperature drop, and on a very thin cylinder insulation helps only once its outer radius passes k/h.

blocks.text: Each layer of a wall has a thermal resistance $\Delta x / k$, a convection film has $1/h$, and in series they add, so the heat flux is the temperature difference divided by the total. The drop across each layer is the flux times its resistance, which makes the **dominant resistance** the layer that decides the heat flow and takes most of the temperature difference. A thick layer of good conductor, such as the copper plate, hardly matters beside a thin layer of insulation, and a film that is everything on a bare surface becomes negligible behind a layer of insulation.

For a pipe the layers have a resistance of $\ln(r_o/r_i)/(2\pi k L)$, which comes from the log mean area, so doubling the insulation's thickness does less than halve the loss. On a very thin wire the **critical radius** $k/h$ marks where insulation starts to pay, and below it more insulation raises the loss.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses the same series resistances inside a heat exchanger, where two films and a tube wall set how much heat passes between two fluids.

lessons.title: Heat exchangers

lead.text: Think about which way the heat flows and where the two fluids meet.

reveal.text: The handbook lists this among the main differences between the two arrangements.

lead.text: In a **counter-flow** exchanger the two fluids move in opposite directions, and in a **parallel-flow** exchanger they move the same way. The handbook lists what follows for parallel flow. The temperature difference between the fluids is largest at the inlet end, which causes thermal stress in the tubes, and the cold fluid can never leave hotter than the coolest temperature of the hot fluid.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the parallel exchanger begins with a difference of 211.1 K and ends with 50.0 K, so most of the surface works against a small driving difference. The counter-flow exchanger keeps the difference between 105.6 K and 155.5 K, which is more even, and it lets the cold fluid leave nearly as hot as the hot fluid enters. The same four temperatures are possible in parallel flow only because the cold outlet, 154.4 °C, is below the hot outlet, 204.4 °C.

The handbook concludes that counter-flow removes more heat under comparable conditions. It gives one reason to choose parallel flow: it suits two fluids that should finish at nearly equal temperatures.

diagram.alt: Two graphs of temperature along a heat exchanger. In parallel flow the hot fluid falls from 260 to 204.4 degrees Celsius while the cold fluid rises from 48.9 to 154.4, and the gap between them shrinks from 211.1 kelvin to 50 kelvin. In counter-flow the gap is 105.6 kelvin at the hot end and 155.5 at the cold end.
diagram.caption: The hot fluid is the upper line in each view and the cold fluid the lower. The dotted brackets mark the temperature difference at each end.

lead.text: Check each proposal against the limit on the cold fluid's outlet.

reveal.text: The same test settles a data sheet: if the cold outlet is above the hot outlet, the arrangement has to be counter-flow.

lead.text: The temperature difference between the fluids changes along the exchanger, and the rate at which heat crosses the tube wall at each point follows the difference at that point. The handbook defines the average that gives the right total, the **log mean temperature difference**, as the difference at one end minus the difference at the other, divided by the natural logarithm of their ratio.

Each end difference pairs the two fluids found at that end. In counter-flow the hot inlet sits opposite the cold outlet, and in parallel flow it sits opposite the cold inlet. The heat transferred is then $Q = U A \Delta T_{lm}$, where $U$ is the overall coefficient built up on the next screens. The handbook states two assumptions behind the log mean: the specific heats of the fluids do not vary much with temperature, and the convection coefficients stay roughly constant along the exchanger.

steps.headline: Find the log mean temperature difference in counter-flow, with the cold fluid warming from 48.9 to 154.4 °C and the hot fluid cooling from 260.0 to 204.4 °C.

lead.text: This is the handbook's liquid-to-liquid counter-flow case converted to SI units.

workedSteps.text: In counter-flow the hot inlet sits opposite the cold outlet, which gives the difference at that end.
At the other end the hot outlet sits opposite the cold inlet.
The numerator is the difference between the two end differences.
The denominator is the natural logarithm of their ratio.
Divide the numerator by the denominator.
The handbook gets 232 °F for this case, which is a temperature difference of 128.9 K.

steps.headline: Find the log mean temperature difference when the same four temperatures are reached in parallel flow.

lead.text: The fluids now enter together at one end and leave together at the other, with the same inlet and outlet temperatures as before.

workedSteps.text: The two inlets are at one end.
The two outlets are at the other end.
Work out the log mean of the two end differences.
This is lower than the 128.9 K of counter-flow, because the difference shrinks to 50.0 K at the outlet end.

lead.text: The heat transferred is $U A \Delta T_{lm}$, and both exchangers must transfer the same heat.

reveal.text: The plain average of the end differences is 130.6 K in both arrangements, so it would have called them equal. Only the log mean separates them, and it is the smaller of the two averages. Sizing the parallel exchanger with the plain average would leave it about 14% short of the area it needs.

lead.text: Between the two fluids the heat crosses three resistances in series: the film on one side of the tube, the tube wall and the film on the other side. The previous lesson, 'Thermal resistance in series', added resistances in this way, and here the sum gives the **overall heat transfer coefficient** $U$, which is the reciprocal of the total. For a thin wall the three areas are nearly equal, and the handbook's thin-wall form is the one below, with $h_1$ and $h_2$ the two film coefficients, $\Delta r$ the wall thickness and $k$ its conductivity.
With $U$ known, $Q = U A \Delta T_{lm}$ gives the heat passed through a tube surface of area $A$. A larger $U$ means less area for the same duty.

steps.headline: Find U for a condenser tube with an inside film of 11,400 W/(m² K) and an outside film of 8,500 W/(m² K), and the heat it passes per metre.

lead.text: This is the handbook's copper condenser tube converted to SI units: 19.05 mm outside diameter, a wall 2.54 mm thick with $k$ = 346 W/(m K), and the log mean difference of 128.9 K found for the counter-flow case.

workedSteps.text: Each film contributes 1/h, and the wall contributes its thickness divided by its conductivity. The values are in units of 10⁻⁵ m²K/W.
The three resistances add.
U is the reciprocal of the total.
The handbook's 827.6 Btu/(hr ft² °F) is the same coefficient in other units.
One metre of tube has an outer surface of π times its diameter, and the heat per metre is U times that area times the log mean difference.
The handbook's 37,700 Btu/(hr ft) is 36.2 kW/m, the same result within rounding.

lead.text: The tube's three resistances are 8.77, 0.73 and 11.76 in units of 10⁻⁵ m²K/W, so the inside film holds 41% of the total, the wall 3% and the outside film 55%. The same reasoning as for a wall applies: a change helps in proportion to the share of the resistance it removes. Doubling the outside coefficient halves the largest resistance and raises $U$ to 6,498 W/(m² K), a gain of 38%, while doubling the inside coefficient raises it to 5,922, a gain of 26%.

afterFigure.text: With a thin wall, the film with the smaller $h$ has the larger resistance. It is the **limiting film**, since it limits $U$ more, and it is the one to improve first. The gain is bounded even so, because the other resistances remain: if the outside film were removed altogether, $U$ could rise only to 10,520 W/(m² K).

diagram.alt: Three stacked bars of the three series resistances of a condenser tube, in units of ten to the minus five square metre kelvin per watt. As built the inside film is 8.8, the wall 0.7 and the outside film 11.8, giving U of 4,701. Doubling the outside film coefficient shortens the bar more than doubling the inside film coefficient.

reveal.text: Improving the weaker film raised U by 77%, and improving the stronger one would have raised it by 7%.

lead.text: A designer wants a quick gain in U from the condenser tube.

reveal.text: A change to a layer that holds 3% of the resistance cannot move U by much.

blocks.text: A cold fluid is to be heated from 48.9 °C to 154.4 °C by a hot fluid that enters at 260.0 °C and leaves at 204.4 °C. The DOE handbook works this liquid-to-liquid case with the two fluids flowing in opposite directions, and the same four temperatures can be reached with them flowing the same way instead. The figure shows both arrangements.

The two exchangers do the same job, and yet the one with the fluids flowing the same way needs about 15% more tube area. The reason lies in how the temperature difference between the fluids changes along the tubes, and in how that difference is averaged to find the heat transferred.

intro.whyItMatters: It decides how large an exchanger has to be and which side of it is worth improving.

recap.keyIdea: Counter-flow keeps the temperature difference more even than parallel flow and so needs less area, the heat transferred is U A times the log mean difference, and U is limited most by the film with the smaller h.

blocks.text: In counter-flow the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid does, and the temperature difference stays more even, so it transfers more heat for the same area than parallel flow, which suits two fluids that are to end near one temperature. The heat transferred is $Q = U A \Delta T_{lm}$, with the log mean found from the two end differences, and the plain average of those differences overstates the driving difference in either arrangement.

$U$ is the reciprocal of the films' and the wall's resistances in series, so an improvement pays in proportion to the share of the resistance it removes. A thin metal wall holds little of it, and the film with the smaller $h$ limits $U$ and is the one to improve first.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the fuel through a whole power station and asks where the energy that does not become electricity goes.

lessons.title: Following the fuel through a power station

lead.text: EIA presents the **heat rate** as a measure of how efficiently a generator or plant turns fuel into heat and then into electricity. It is the energy the plant uses to generate one kilowatt-hour, in Btu per net kilowatt-hour. **Net generation** is the electricity a plant supplies to the transmission line, after the electricity its own equipment uses, which covers fuel feeders, boiler pumps, cooling equipment and emission controls.

A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 MJ, which EIA writes as 3,412 Btu, so the efficiency is that figure divided by the heat rate. EIA's own examples are a heat rate of 10,500 Btu, which is an efficiency of 33%, and one of 7,500 Btu, which is 45%. A lower heat rate means less fuel for each kilowatt-hour, so it is the better figure.

reveal.text: The result is the figure used for coal from here on.

lead.text: EIA's 2025 averages put the four fuels in two groups. Natural gas plants used 7,781 Btu for each kilowatt-hour, which is 43.9% efficiency, and coal, petroleum and nuclear plants used between 10,443 and 10,969 Btu, which is 31.1% to 32.7%. In SI units a kilowatt-hour sent out took 8.2 MJ of fuel energy at a gas plant and 11.0 to 11.6 MJ at the others, and the figure draws the bars to scale.

afterFigure.text: These **fleet averages** are taken over the plants in operation, so they describe the whole fleet, old units and new. For coal, petroleum and natural gas, EIA averages over the plants of utilities and independent power producers, and it leaves out combined heat and power plants and any commercial or industrial plant. The nuclear figure is built differently, as the weighted average of the tested heat rates of nuclear units.

diagram.alt: Four horizontal bars of fuel energy for each kilowatt-hour sent out in 2025: coal 10,647 Btu or 11.2 megajoules, petroleum 10,969 or 11.6, natural gas 7,781 or 8.2, and nuclear 10,443 or 11.0. In each, the first 3.6 megajoules are shaded as electricity, giving efficiencies of 32.0, 31.1, 43.9 and 32.7 percent.

steps.headline: Find the power that a 600 MW coal station's fuel carries without delivering it as electricity, using the 2025 average heat rate of 10,647 Btu/kWh.

lead.text: The station sends 600 MW to the grid. The fuel power follows from the ratio of the heat rate to 3,412, because 3,412 Btu is the 1 kWh that leaves as electricity.

workedSteps.text: The fuel energy for each kWh of electricity is the heat rate divided by 3,412.
workedSteps.math: 10,647 ÷ 3,412 = 3.12 kWh of fuel for each kWh sent out

workedSteps.text: The fuel power is that ratio times the electrical power.
The part that does not leave as electricity is the difference.
That is 68% of the fuel power, the complement of the coal plant's 32.0% efficiency.

steps.headline: Find the power that a 600 MW gas station's fuel carries without delivering it as electricity, using the 2025 average heat rate of 7,781 Btu/kWh.

lead.text: The same steps apply with the gas plant's heat rate.

workedSteps.text: The fuel energy for each kWh of electricity is the heat rate divided by 3,412.
workedSteps.math: 7,781 ÷ 3,412 = 2.28 kWh of fuel for each kWh sent out

workedSteps.text: The fuel power is that ratio times 600 MW.
The part that does not leave as electricity is the difference. Work out how many megawatts it is.
That is 56% of the fuel power, against 68% for the coal station, so the gas station sends less heat away for the same output.

lead.text: Energy that does not leave a station as electricity leaves as heat, and for a heat engine that is required. The DOE handbook notes that even in its ideal cycle only part of the heat taken in is available to the engine, because the rest has to be rejected to the environment, so **rejected heat** is no sign of a poor design. The handbook adds that the ideal efficiency depends only on the source and sink temperatures, and that a real plant is limited at both ends: the earth is its final heat sink, and the materials of the boiler limit how hot the source can be.

In a steam plant the rejection happens in the condenser, which the handbook describes as the cycle's heat-rejection mechanism, and the heat passes to the cooling water. The handbook also describes a cooling tower, in which part of the water evaporates into the air passing through. Wikipedia's article on the Rankine cycle says that the water vapour with condensed droplets often seen above power stations comes from the cooling systems and not directly from the closed steam cycle. The sources used here do not say how the rejected heat divides between the condenser, the stack and other losses, so the lesson makes no estimate of that division.
Think about where the rejected heat is carried away.

reveal.text: A cooling tower cools its water by letting part of it evaporate into the air, so the plume is made at the cooling system and not in the steam loop.

lead.text: Between 2015 and 2025 the average heat rate for gas plants fell from 7,869 to 7,781 Btu/kWh, a drop of 1.1%, so gas plants burned slightly less fuel for each kilowatt-hour. Coal rose from 10,495 to 10,647 Btu/kWh, which is 1.4% more fuel, petroleum from 10,687 to 10,969, which is 2.6% more, and nuclear fell from 10,458 to 10,443, a drop of 0.1%.

afterFigure.text: A rising heat rate is a falling efficiency, so the coal fleet slipped from 32.5% to 32.0% over the decade. The changes are small beside the gap between gas and the other fuels, and an average over all the plants running cannot show how well a new plant performs, because the older units are in it too.

reveal.text: A falling heat rate means less fuel for each kilowatt-hour, which is the improvement.

lead.text: A stated efficiency can be tested before it is believed, with three questions. The first is whether it sits below the [[Carnot limit|The greatest efficiency any heat engine can reach between a source and a sink at two given temperatures. Met in 'Testing a claimed efficiency'.]]. The DOE handbook takes a heat source of about 816 °C, the practical limit it gives for boilers, and a sink of about 16 °C, and gets 73.5%, which it says is far beyond what any real system can do.

The second question is whether it is near what plants of that type achieve. Wikipedia's article on combined cycles puts a single-cycle steam plant at 35 to 42% at most, reports that Guinness World Records certified the world's most efficient combined-cycle plant at 62.22% in 2016, and gives around 64% as best-of-class in base-load operation. The third question is what the figure is measured against. The same article gives one combined-cycle station as nearly 60% on the lower heating value of the fuel and 54% on the higher, and EIA's heat rates count net generation. The EIA pages used here do not say which heating value its heat rates use, so a claim has to name its basis before it can be compared.

afterFigure.text: The handbook's own 1992 figures, about 40% for fossil plants and about 31% for nuclear, differ from EIA's 2025 fleet averages of 32.0% for coal and 32.7% for nuclear, and the sources do not say why. They answer different questions, a typical figure in a handbook and a measured average of operating plants, which is a reason to ask what a number measures before comparing it with another.

diagram.alt: A number line of efficiency from 0 to 80 percent with reference points: a band for single-cycle steam plants from 35 to 42 percent, the best certified combined-cycle plant at 62.22 percent, and a Carnot limit of 73.5 percent for a heat source at 816 degrees Celsius and a sink at 16. Below the line, the 2025 fleet averages are petroleum 31.1, coal 32.0, nuclear 32.7 and natural gas 43.9 percent.
diagram.caption: Claimed efficiencies can be placed on this line before they are believed.

blocks.text: In 2025 the average coal plant in the United States used 10,647 Btu of fuel energy for every kilowatt-hour it sent to the transmission line, according to the Energy Information Administration. A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 MJ, which EIA writes as 3,412 Btu, so the fuel carried about three times the energy of the electricity that came out, as the figure shows to scale.

The rest of that energy went somewhere. EIA reports one number per plant for the fuel it takes to send out a kilowatt-hour, and that number is enough to estimate the heat the plant has to get rid of and to test a claimed efficiency against what plants are known to achieve.

diagram.alt: A bar for one kilowatt-hour sent out by an average coal plant in 2025. The bar is 11.23 megajoules of fuel energy long, and the first 3.6 megajoules, shaded green, leave as electricity. The remaining 7.63 megajoules do not leave as electricity.
diagram.caption: The bar is drawn to scale. EIA reports the fuel energy as 10,647 Btu for each kilowatt-hour.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a heat rate into an efficiency and a heat load, and say whether a stated efficiency is believable.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you check a power station's figures before you rely on them.

recap.keyIdea: A heat rate gives the efficiency as 3,412 divided by it, the fuel energy that does not leave as electricity is heat that the second law requires a plant to reject, and a stated efficiency has to pass the Carnot limit, the range for its plant type and the basis it is measured on.

blocks.text: The heat rate is the fuel energy a plant uses for each kilowatt-hour sent out, and dividing 3,412 Btu by it gives the efficiency. For the 2025 averages that is 43.9% for gas and between 31.1% and 32.7% for the others, and the fuel energy that does not leave as electricity, 56% to 69% of the total, is heat that goes to the condenser and the cooling system. The white plume over a station is vapour from the cooling system and not the closed steam loop.

A fleet average covers old and new units, so it describes the fleet and sets no ceiling for a new plant. A stated efficiency should sit below the Carnot limit, near the range for its plant type, and be quoted on a stated basis, which is why 57% for a steam plant fails although it is under 73.5%.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns capacity ratings into the energy a plant delivers over a year and compares ways of heating a home by the fuel they burn.

lessons.title: Judging energy claims

lead.text: A station's capacity is the power it delivers at full output, but the energy it delivers over a year depends on how often it runs. EIA's glossary defines the **capacity factor** as the electrical energy a unit produced over a period divided by what it would have produced running continuously at full power for the same period.

A year has 8,760 hours, so a 100 MW unit running at full power throughout would deliver 876 GWh, and the energy it really delivers is that times its capacity factor. EIA's annual figures for 2025 were 91.1% for nuclear, 58.7% for gas combined-cycle plants, 48.8% for coal, 34.4% for hydroelectric, 33.8% for wind, 24.0% for solar photovoltaic and 13.6% for gas turbines.

afterFigure.text: A capacity factor measures how much a unit ran, and it is not an efficiency. Gas combined-cycle plants ran at 58.7% in 2025 and gas turbines at 13.6%, and the gap says how much each kind of unit was used. It says nothing about how well either converts fuel to electricity, which is what the heat rate of the last lesson measures, and the number alone does not say why a unit ran so little.

diagram.alt: Seven horizontal bars of 2025 annual capacity factors: nuclear 91.1 percent, gas combined cycle 58.7, coal 48.8, hydroelectric 34.4, wind 33.8, solar photovoltaic 24.0 and gas turbine 13.6.
diagram.caption: A bar's length is the share of a full year at full power that the technology's units delivered on average.

lead.text: Turn a rating into the energy delivered over a year.

reveal.text: A rating says what a unit can deliver at its best. The capacity factor says how much of that it delivered.

lead.text: A commentator reads a capacity factor as a measure of quality.

reveal.text: The number records how much a unit ran and gives no reason for it.

steps.headline: Find how many MW of solar photovoltaic capacity deliver as much energy in a year as 100 MW of nuclear, using the 2025 capacity factors of 91.1% and 24.0%.

lead.text: Equal annual energy means that capacity times capacity factor is the same on both sides, because the hours in the year are the same. The comparison is of energy over the year, and it says nothing about when the energy arrives.

workedSteps.text: First the energy of the nuclear unit over a year.
The solar capacity C has to deliver the same energy at a factor of 24.0%.
The hours cancel, and C is the nuclear capacity times the ratio of the two factors.
Solar needs 3.8 times the nuclear capacity to deliver the same energy over the year.

steps.headline: Find how many MW of wind capacity deliver as much energy in a year as 100 MW of nuclear, using the 2025 capacity factors of 91.1% and 33.8%.

lead.text: The same steps apply with wind's capacity factor.

workedSteps.text: The nuclear unit delivers the same 798 GWh as before.
The wind capacity C must deliver that at a factor of 33.8%.
Solve for C. Work out how many megawatts of wind it is.
That is 2.7 times the nuclear capacity, against 3.8 times for solar photovoltaic.

steps.headline: Fuel for a kilowatt-hour of heat

lead.text: Heat can come from a resistance heater, a heat pump or a boiler, and the fuel that has to be burned to make a kilowatt-hour of it, its **primary energy**, depends on what stands behind each. Wikipedia gives an electrical resistance heater a [[COP|Coefficient of performance: the heat delivered for each unit of electricity used. Met in 'Moving heat with work'.]] of 1.0 and a well-designed heat pump typically a COP of 3 to 5, with 10 °C outside and 20 °C inside. Suppose the electricity comes from gas plants at the 2025 average heat rate of 7,781 Btu/kWh. Each kilowatt-hour of electricity then took 7,781 ÷ 3,412 = 2.28 kWh of fuel, and a heat pump with COP $c$ delivers $c$ kWh of heat for it, so the fuel for each kWh of heat is 2.28 ÷ $c$.

afterFigure.text: On that grid a resistance heater takes 2.28 kWh of fuel for each kWh of heat, a heat pump with COP 3 takes 0.76, and a boiler that is 90% efficient takes 1 ÷ 0.90 = 1.11. These counts leave out the losses in transmitting electricity, because the sources used here give no figure for them, and they take the boiler's 90% as stated, since the source does not say which heating value it refers to.

diagram.alt: A graph of the fuel burned for each kilowatt-hour of heat against heat pump COP from 1 to 5, on a grid supplied by gas plants at 7,781 Btu per kilowatt-hour. The curve falls from 2.28 kilowatt-hours at COP 1 to 0.76 at COP 3, and crosses the gas boiler's 1.11 at a COP of 2.05.
diagram.caption: The heat pump's fuel is 2.28 divided by its COP. The dashed line is the boiler. Grid losses are ignored.

steps.headline: Find the COP at which a heat pump burns the same fuel for each kWh of heat as a 90% efficient gas boiler, on a grid supplied by gas plants at 7,781 Btu/kWh.

lead.text: Grid losses are ignored, as before.

workedSteps.text: The fuel for a kWh of electricity on this grid is the heat rate divided by 3,412.
The boiler takes the reciprocal of its efficiency in fuel for each kWh of heat.
The heat pump matches the boiler when the electricity's fuel divided by the COP equals the boiler's.
Solve for the COP.
Above a COP of about 2, the heat pump burns less fuel than the boiler on this grid, and below it burns more.

lead.text: Run the same comparison on a grid of coal plants.

reveal.text: A dirtier grid raises the break-even COP, so the same heat pump can beat the boiler on one grid and lose to it on another.

lead.text: Emissions follow the same arithmetic, with the emissions per kilowatt-hour of the energy source in place of the heat rate. For a boiler, the emissions for a kWh of heat are the source's figure divided by the efficiency, 201 g ÷ 0.90 = 223 g. For a heat pump they are the electricity's figure divided by the COP: 1,221 g ÷ 3 = 407 g for the lignite electricity, 436 g ÷ 4 = 109 g for the global mix in 2022, and 11 g ÷ 4 = 3 g for onshore wind.

The same division gives the COP a heat pump needs to match the boiler's 223 g, which is about 1.95 on the global mix and about 5.5 on the lignite electricity, above the 3 to 5 that Wikipedia gives as typical for a well-designed heat pump. The article sums up the result: the footprint of a heat pump depends on how its electricity is made, and heat pumps usually still cut emissions.
Read the table's rows against each other.

reveal.text: Both numbers in the lignite row are right. What changes the verdict is the electricity behind the heat pump.

lead.text: A claimed COP can be tested against the Carnot limit before any data is asked for. For heat delivered at $T_h$ from a source at $T_c$, both in kelvin, the limit is $T_h / (T_h - T_c)$, as in 'Moving heat with work'. For heat delivered at 35 °C from a source at 0 °C it is 308 ÷ 35 = 8.8, and the best real unit in the Wikipedia table for those conditions, a high-efficiency air-source heat pump, reaches 3.8. A claim above the limit is impossible. A claim between the best real unit and the limit is allowed by the physics, and it lies far beyond what the table shows, which is a reason to ask for test results and no reason to reject it outright.

A quoted saving needs reading as closely as a quoted COP. The US Department of Energy says that modern air-source heat pumps can cut electricity use by 50% against furnaces and baseboard heaters. The sentence is about electricity use, and "can" marks a saving that is possible. If the heater it replaces is a resistance heater with a COP of 1.0, then half the electricity for the same heat means an average COP near 2 over the season, but that is an inference from the sentence and not a figure the Department gives.
Apply the limit to a different source temperature.

reveal.text: The Carnot test would pass a COP of 6 for air at 0 °C, where the limit is 8.8, so a claim has to name both temperatures.

lead.text: A quoted saving can be read too broadly.

reveal.text: The sentence is careful: it says what can fall, against what, and by how much. A reader who drops those words has made a different claim.

lessons.orientation: Turn capacity ratings into annual energy, compare heating options by the fuel they burn, and test claims against the limits that apply.
lessons.nextAction: Check an energy claim you have met recently against the limits from this course.

blocks.text: A table in the Wikipedia article on heat pumps compares four ways of making a kilowatt-hour of heat, and the figure draws its results. A gas boiler that is 90% efficient comes to 223 g of carbon dioxide, a heat pump with a COP of 4 on the global electricity mix to 109 g, the same heat pump on onshore wind to 3 g, and a heat pump with a COP of 3 on electricity from an old lignite plant to 407 g.

The heat pump on the global mix beats the boiler and the one on lignite electricity loses to it, and both rows are correct. Every row comes from dividing one stated figure by another, and a claim about energy can be tested the same way, by finding the figures it rests on: how much a plant runs, how much fuel a kilowatt-hour of heat takes, and what the physics allows.

diagram.alt: Four horizontal bars of carbon dioxide emitted for each kilowatt-hour of heat: a heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 3 on electricity from an old lignite plant, 407 grams; a gas boiler at 90 percent efficiency, 223 grams; a heat pump with a coefficient of 4 on the global electricity mix, 109 grams; and a heat pump with a coefficient of 4 on onshore wind, 3 grams.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn ratings into annual energy, compare heating options by fuel, and test claims against what the physics allows.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you check an energy claim before you repeat it or act on it.

recap.keyIdea: A capacity factor measures how much a unit ran and turns a rating into annual energy, a heat pump's fuel for heat is its electricity's fuel divided by its COP, and a claim has to stay under the Carnot limit and near what real units achieve.

blocks.text: Annual energy is capacity times 8,760 hours times the capacity factor, so the same energy from a technology with a lower factor takes proportionally more capacity, and the factor says nothing of efficiency or of when the energy arrives. A kilowatt-hour of heat from a heat pump takes the electricity's fuel, the grid's heat rate over 3,412, divided by the COP, and the heat pump beats a 90% boiler on fuel only above a break-even COP that rises as the grid gets dirtier.

The same division gives emissions, so a heat pump can beat a gas boiler on one grid and lose to it on another. A claimed COP must lie below the Carnot limit for its temperatures and, to be believed, near what real units reach, and a quoted saving has to be read for what it compares and what it says can happen.
