questions.prompt: An engineer wants the shaft power that the feed pump needs, and she knows the state of the water going into the pump and coming out of it. Which boundary should she draw?
hints: Ask which boundary has the pump's shaft work crossing it and the fewest other unknowns.
She knows the state of the water only at the pump's inlet and at its outlet.

acceptedIdeas: Round the pump alone, with water crossing at its inlet and outlet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Round the pump alone, with water crossing at its inlet and outlet

choices.label: Round the pump alone, with water crossing at its inlet and outlet
Round the whole loop, so that no water crosses the boundary
Round the boiler alone, since the boiler receives the water that the pump delivers
Round the condenser and pump together, since the water passes through both in turn

questions.onCorrect: The pump alone suits the question: the water's state is known where it crosses, and the shaft work is the one energy term left to find.

misconceptions.feedback: With the whole loop inside, the pump's work is one term among several, alongside the heat at the boiler, the heat at the condenser and the turbine's work, and she knows none of the others.
The pump's shaft does not cross the boiler's boundary, so its work never appears in that balance. Only the water arriving from the pump does.
That adds the condenser's heat to the balance, and she has no figure for it. A smaller boundary leaves the pump's work as the only unknown energy term.

questions.prompt: A steam turbine's casing is taken as the boundary. Steam enters and leaves, the shaft turns a generator, and a little heat leaks out through the casing. What type of system is this?
hints: Name each thing that crosses the casing: steam, shaft, heat.
A closed system allows no mass to cross.

acceptedIdeas: Open, because steam crosses along with work and heat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open, because steam crosses along with work and heat

choices.label: Closed, because the casing is sealed against leaks
Isolated, because the casing is insulated against heat loss
Open, because steam crosses along with work and heat
Closed, because the same steam goes round the plant again

questions.onCorrect: Steam crosses along with work and heat, so mass, heat and work all cross: the turbine is an open system.

misconceptions.feedback: A sealed casing describes the machine, but the type of system is set by what crosses the boundary. Steam crosses at the inlet and the outlet, so mass does cross.
Insulation reduces the heat that crosses and leaves the shaft work and the steam as they are. An isolated system has no mass, heat or work crossing at all.
The water does recirculate, but this boundary is drawn round the turbine alone, and steam crosses it at the inlet and at the outlet.

questions.prompt: A boundary is drawn round a feed pump, with the pump's motor outside it. Sort each item by what it is for this boundary.
hints: Ask first whether the item is matter, energy in transit or a property of the water.
Energy that crosses without matter is either shaft work or heat, and heat needs a temperature difference.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Water in and out is mass, shaft power is work, warmth through the casing is heat, and the pressure rise and the motor's electricity do not cross.

items.label: Water entering at the inlet
items.explanation: Matter crossing the boundary is mass flow, and it carries energy with it.

items.label: Water leaving at the outlet
items.explanation: Mass flow leaves with its energy too, so the outlet is a crossing.

items.label: Shaft power arriving from the motor
items.explanation: A shaft turning against the water puts work into the system.

items.label: Warmth escaping from the casing into the room
items.explanation: Energy that crosses because of a temperature difference, and is neither mass flow nor shaft work, is heat.

items.label: The rise in the water's pressure
items.explanation: Pressure is a property of the water inside the boundary. It is a result of the work, not something that crosses.

items.label: Electricity feeding the motor
items.explanation: The motor lies outside this boundary, so only its shaft power crosses.

questions.onCorrect: Mass: water in and water out. Work: shaft power. Heat: warmth through the casing. Does not cross: the pressure rise and the motor's electricity.

questions.prompt: Why is the heat leaking from the turbine's casing written with a minus sign?
hints: Recall which direction of heat the convention counts as positive.
Ask whether this energy is entering the boundary or leaving it.

acceptedIdeas: Heat into the system is positive, and this heat is leaving the system
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heat into the system is positive, and this heat is leaving the system

choices.label: Because it is a loss, and a loss is always counted as a negative term
Heat into the system is positive, and this heat is leaving the system
Because heat is always counted as negative when the machine is a turbine

questions.onCorrect: The convention counts heat into the system as positive, so heat leaving through the casing is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: Whether a term is negative depends on its direction relative to the system, under the stated convention, and has nothing to do with whether it is wasted. The turbine's useful work leaves the system and is positive.
The sign follows the direction of the crossing. A turbine that was being warmed from outside would have positive heat in the same convention.

questions.prompt: A feed pump takes 6 kW of shaft power and passes it to the water. With heat into the system and work out of the system counted as positive, what is the pump's work term?
hints: Is the shaft power entering the boundary or leaving it?
Work out of the system is the positive direction.

acceptedIdeas: −6 kW
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: −6 kW

choices.label: +6 kW
−6 kW
0 kW

questions.onCorrect: The pump puts work into the water, which is work into the system, so the term is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the work term for a machine doing work on its surroundings, such as a turbine. The pump has work done on its water, which is work into the system.
The shaft crosses the boundary carrying power, so the work term is not zero. Only its sign has to be settled.

questions.prompt: The same pump loses 0.3 kW of heat through its casing to the room. With heat into the system counted as positive, what is the heat term, in kW?
hints: Is this heat entering the boundary or leaving it?
Heat into the system is positive, so a heat loss takes the opposite sign.
Write the size of the leak with that sign in front.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The heat leaves the system, and heat into the system is positive, so the heat term is −0.3 kW.

questions.onCorrect: The casing's heat leaves the system, so it enters the balance as −0.3 kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the leak. Heat leaving the system is counted as negative.
That is the pump's shaft power, a work term. The question asks for the heat term.

questions.prompt: A boundary is drawn round the turbine and the condenser together, with the exhaust steam passing from one to the other inside it. Which statement about this boundary is right?
hints: Follow the water: where does it enter the pair of machines, and where does it leave?
Then list what else reaches through the boundary: the shaft, and the heat at the condenser.

acceptedIdeas: Open: steam enters the turbine, water leaves the condenser, and work and heat cross as well
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open: steam enters the turbine, water leaves the condenser, and work and heat cross as well

choices.label: Open: steam enters the turbine, water leaves the condenser, and work and heat cross as well
Closed: the exhaust passes from turbine to condenser inside the boundary, so no mass crosses
Closed: only heat and work cross, since the water stays inside the two machines
Isolated: the two machines are joined, so nothing crosses between them and the surroundings

questions.onCorrect: Mass crosses at the turbine inlet and the condenser outlet, with work and heat as well, so the pair is open. The exhaust passing between them is internal.

misconceptions.feedback: That flow is internal, but steam still enters at the turbine inlet and water leaves at the condenser outlet. Mass crosses the boundary at its two ends.
The water does not stay inside. It enters the pair as steam and leaves it as condensate, so mass crosses the boundary.
The joint between the machines is internal, but the shaft carries work out and the condenser rejects heat, so energy does cross.

questions.prompt: A diesel engine's lubricating oil is pumped through the engine and then through an oil cooler, which passes heat to cooling water on the far side of its tubes. An engineer draws a boundary round the oil inside the cooler. Which description fits that system?
hints: Name what enters and leaves at the two ends of the tubes.
The cooler exists to move energy to the water, so ask how that energy crosses the boundary.

acceptedIdeas: Open: oil crosses at both ends and heat crosses the tube walls to the water
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Open: oil crosses at both ends and heat crosses the tube walls to the water

choices.label: Open: oil crosses at both ends and heat crosses the tube walls to the water
Closed: the oil is sealed in the tubes, so only heat can reach the cooling water
Isolated: the tube walls keep the oil and the cooling water apart
Closed: the same oil circulates through the engine and returns to the cooler

questions.onCorrect: Oil enters and leaves, and the heat it gives up crosses the tube walls, so the oil in the cooler is an open system with heat leaving.

misconceptions.feedback: The tubes are sealed against leaks, but oil still enters at one end and leaves at the other, so mass crosses the boundary.
The walls stop the two liquids mixing, and they carry the heat that the cooler exists to remove. That heat crosses the boundary.
The oil does return, but this boundary is drawn round the cooler alone, and oil crosses it at the inlet and at the outlet.

questions.prompt: A drawing carries the note 'The steam in this vessel holds 500 kJ of heat and 200 kJ of work.' What is the best correction to it, given this passage?
hints: Look at what the passage says systems never possess.
Ask what the steam does store, and what heat and work are while they happen.

extracts.text: Systems never possess heat or work, but either or both may occur when a system undergoes a change of energy state. Both heat and work are boundary phenomena in that both are observed at the boundary of the system.
extracts.who: U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Fundamentals Handbook: Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Flow, Volume 1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92)
extracts.kind: A US government fundamentals handbook for plant operators

acceptedIdeas: Neither is held: the steam stores internal energy, and heat and work only cross
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Neither is held: the steam stores internal energy, and heat and work only cross

choices.label: Heat is held by the steam, and work is held by the shaft that drives the pump
Both are held by the steam, so the two can be added to give its total energy content
Only heat is held by the steam, because a temperature difference stores energy
Neither is held: the steam stores internal energy, and heat and work only cross

questions.onCorrect: Heat and work are boundary phenomena, so the note should give the steam's internal energy and treat heat and work as crossings.

misconceptions.feedback: A shaft does not hold work either. Work is energy crossing the boundary while the shaft turns against a load, and the passage says a system never possesses it.
Neither is held, so there is nothing to add. What the steam stores is internal energy, with kinetic and potential energy if it moves or is raised.
Heat is not held either. A hot body stores internal energy, and heat exists only while energy crosses a boundary because of a temperature difference.

questions.prompt: An operator wants the heat that a whole steam plant takes in at its boiler for a given net electrical output. She has no figures for the steam between the machines. Which boundary suits her question?
hints: Which boundary hides the steam states between the machines?
She wants heat in at the boiler and net work out, so both must cross the boundary she draws.

acceptedIdeas: Round all four machines, so only heat and net work cross the boundary
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Round all four machines, so only heat and net work cross the boundary

choices.label: Round the turbine alone, so the steam's state at its ends gives the work
Round all four machines, so only heat and net work cross the boundary
Round the boiler alone, since that is where the heat enters
Round the condenser alone, since the heat it rejects matches the heat taken in

questions.onCorrect: With every machine inside, the unknown steam states never cross the boundary, and the heat in, heat out and net work do.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs the steam's state at both ends of the turbine, which she does not have, and it says nothing about the heat taken in at the boiler.
The boiler's balance contains the enthalpy of the steam leaving it, which she does not know, and no work crosses that boundary at all.
The rejected heat is smaller than the heat taken in by the net work, and the condenser's own steam states are unknown to her as well.

questions.prompt: A small steam turbine delivers 2,400 kW to a generator, and 45 kW of heat leaks from its casing into the room. A boundary is drawn round the casing, with heat into the system and work out of the system counted as positive. What is the heat term, in kW?
hints: Which of the two numbers is a heat flow, and which is work?
Is that heat entering the boundary or leaving it?
Heat into the system is positive, so heat leaving takes the opposite sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The heat leaves the system, so with heat into the system counted as positive the term is −45 kW. The 2,400 kW is the work term, +2,400 kW.

questions.onCorrect: The 45 kW of heat leaves the system, so it enters the balance as −45 kW, while the work term is +2,400 kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the leak. Heat leaving the system is negative in this convention.
That is the work term, and work out of the system is positive. The question asks for the heat term.
That mixes up the two terms. The 2,400 kW is work out, so it is +2,400 kW, and the heat term is separate.

questions.prompt: A pan of water is boiling at 100 °C on an open stove, and the burner stays on. What does a thermometer in the water read a few minutes later, while some water is still left?
hints: Recall what happens to the temperature of a substance while it changes phase.
The burner keeps supplying heat, so ask where that energy is going.

acceptedIdeas: It stays at about 100 °C, since the heat goes into boiling the water
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays at about 100 °C, since the heat goes into boiling the water

choices.label: It stays at about 100 °C, since the heat goes into boiling the water
It keeps rising, though more slowly, as the water takes in more heat
It rises faster, because the steam above the water holds the heat in
It falls a little, because boiling carries energy away from the water

questions.onCorrect: The temperature holds at the boiling point while liquid remains, because the heat goes into turning liquid to vapour.

misconceptions.feedback: At a fixed pressure the temperature of boiling water stays at the saturation temperature however much heat arrives, until the last of the liquid has gone.
The heat from the burner goes into turning liquid into vapour, and the steam above the pan does not raise the temperature of the water below it.
Boiling does carry energy away in the vapour, but the burner replaces it. While liquid remains, the temperature holds at the boiling point.

questions.prompt: The table gives a saturation pressure of 1,554.3 kPa at 200 °C and 1,002.7 kPa at 180 °C. Water at 200 °C is held at 1,000 kPa. Which region is it in?
hints: Look up the saturation pressure at the water's temperature, 200 °C.
Compare it with the pressure the water is actually held at.

acceptedIdeas: Superheated vapour, because 1,000 kPa is below the 1,554.3 kPa that 200 °C needs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Superheated vapour, because 1,000 kPa is below the 1,554.3 kPa that 200 °C needs

choices.label: Compressed liquid, since 1,000 kPa is a high pressure to put on water at 200 °C
Saturated mixture, since 1,000 kPa is close to the 1,002.7 kPa listed for 180 °C
Superheated vapour, because 1,000 kPa is below the 1,554.3 kPa that 200 °C needs

questions.onCorrect: The pressure is below the saturation pressure for 200 °C, so the water is above its boiling point: superheated vapour.

misconceptions.feedback: Compressed liquid at 200 °C needs more than 1,554.3 kPa. At 1,000 kPa the water boils just under 180 °C, so 200 °C is above its boiling point.
The 1,002.7 kPa belongs to 180 °C. At 200 °C a mixture needs 1,554.3 kPa, so at 1,000 kPa the water is hotter than its boiling point and is all vapour.

questions.prompt: Wet steam in a condenser is at 40 °C. What else must you know to fix its state?
hints: In the mixture region, how many different pressures can water have at 40 °C?
Two properties are needed to fix a state. If the first fixes the second, which kind of property is still missing?

acceptedIdeas: Its quality, because 40 °C already fixes the pressure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its quality, because 40 °C already fixes the pressure

choices.label: Nothing more, since 40 °C fixes the state of water
Its pressure, because 40 °C fixes only the temperature
Its quality, because 40 °C already fixes the pressure

questions.onCorrect: The temperature and pressure of a mixture are tied together, so a third property, the quality, says how much of it is vapour.

misconceptions.feedback: At 40 °C the pressure is fixed at 7.370 kPa, but liquid and vapour can be mixed in any proportion there, and the enthalpy changes with the mix.
In the mixture region 40 °C already fixes the pressure, at 7.370 kPa in the table, so the pressure would add no new information.

questions.prompt: Why is only 0.90 of $h_{fg}$ added to $h_f$ in this calculation?
hints: Think about what each kilogram of the mixture has in common, whether it is liquid or vapour.
Ask which part of the mass needs the extra amount to have vaporised.

acceptedIdeas: Every kilogram has the liquid's $h_f$, and only the vapour share needs the extra $h_{fg}$
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every kilogram has the liquid's $h_f$, and only the vapour share needs the extra $h_{fg}$

choices.label: Every kilogram has the liquid's $h_f$, and only the vapour share needs the extra $h_{fg}$
Because a quality of 0.90 means the water is 90% of the way to its boiling temperature
Because 10% of the energy is lost when the liquid and the vapour mix together

questions.onCorrect: All the mass has at least the liquid's enthalpy, and only the fraction $x$ that is vapour has also taken in $h_{fg}$.

misconceptions.feedback: The temperature is already at its boiling point. The quality says what share of the mass has become vapour.
Nothing is lost on mixing. The 0.10 of liquid keeps $h_f$ and needs nothing extra, which is why only the vapour share carries $h_{fg}$.

questions.prompt: To find the quality from a measured enthalpy, you divide the enthalpy above the liquid's value, $h - h_f$, by which table value?
hints: Quality is the fraction of the way from saturated liquid to saturated vapour.
The whole distance between those two ends is one table value.

acceptedIdeas: $h_{fg}$, the enthalpy needed to vaporise the liquid fully
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: $h_{fg}$, the enthalpy needed to vaporise the liquid fully

choices.label: $h_f$, the enthalpy of the saturated liquid at that pressure
$h_g$, the enthalpy of the saturated vapour at that pressure
$h_{fg}$, the enthalpy needed to vaporise the liquid fully

questions.onCorrect: The quality is the fraction of the whole step from saturated liquid to saturated vapour, so the divisor is $h_{fg}$.

misconceptions.feedback: Dividing by $h_f$ compares the energy added with the liquid's own enthalpy. The quality compares it with the energy needed to vaporise everything.
The enthalpy above $h_f$ is spread over the range from $h_f$ to $h_g$, and that range is $h_{fg}$. Dividing by $h_g$ includes the liquid's own enthalpy as well.

questions.prompt: Wet steam at 200 °C has a specific enthalpy of 2,400 kJ/kg, with $h_f = 851.9$ and $h_{fg} = 1{,}937.3$ kJ/kg from the table. What is its quality?
hints: Take the enthalpy above the liquid's value first: $h - h_f$.
Divide that by $h_{fg}$.
The result is a fraction between 0 and 1.
questions.onCorrect: A quality of 0.80 means that 80% of the mass is vapour and 20% is liquid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moisture, the liquid fraction, which is 1 − x. The quality is the vapour fraction.
That divides by $h_f$, which is 851.9. Divide by $h_{fg}$ instead.
That divides by $h_g$, which is 2,789.2. The divisor for quality is $h_{fg}$.

questions.prompt: An engineer puts a gauge reading of 150 kPa and a temperature of 25 °C straight into $Pv = RT$ to find the density of air in a tank. What is wrong with this?
hints: Ask what a gauge reading of zero actually means about the gas inside.
Ask where each scale puts its zero.

acceptedIdeas: Both must be absolute: add the atmosphere to the gauge reading and use kelvin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both must be absolute: add the atmosphere to the gauge reading and use kelvin

choices.label: Only the temperature needs converting, since a gauge already measures pressure
Only the gauge reading needs correcting, since a Celsius offset is small
Both must be absolute: add the atmosphere to the gauge reading and use kelvin
Nothing is wrong, since the law holds in any consistent set of units

questions.onCorrect: The law counts from true zero, so the pressure must be gauge plus atmosphere and the temperature must be in kelvin.

misconceptions.feedback: A gauge reads the pressure above the atmosphere. The gas law needs the whole pressure of the gas, so the atmosphere has to be added to the reading.
An offset of 273 is not small beside 25 °C. Using 25 as the temperature would be wrong by a factor of about twelve.
The law also needs zero to be the true zero of pressure and of temperature, and neither a gauge nor a Celsius scale puts it there.

questions.prompt: Which of these can an engineer treat as an ideal gas without much worry?
hints: Which state is far from condensing, and at a modest pressure?
Think about the two conditions the model needs: well above saturation, and a pressure that is not high.

acceptedIdeas: Air at room temperature, at atmospheric pressure, far from condensing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Air at room temperature, at atmospheric pressure, far from condensing

choices.label: Steam at 22 MPa and 374 °C, close to water's critical point
Saturated steam at 200 °C, in contact with boiling water at 1,554.3 kPa
Air at room temperature, at atmospheric pressure, far from condensing

questions.onCorrect: Air at room conditions is far above its condensation temperature at a modest pressure, which is where the ideal gas model is safe.

misconceptions.feedback: At 22.1 MPa the forces between molecules are large, and the gas law fails badly close to the critical point.
At that state the gas law's density is 9.5% below the table's, and a small drop in temperature starts to condense the steam.

questions.prompt: An operator's log carries the entry 'Saturated steam, 150 °C, 300 kPa'. The table gives a saturation pressure of 476.0 kPa at 150 °C. What is the fair reading of the entry?
hints: For saturated water at 150 °C, what pressure does the table give?
Compare the logged pressure with that, and decide which region the logged pair really describes.

acceptedIdeas: Inconsistent: saturated steam at 150 °C is at 476.0 kPa, so a figure or the label is wrong
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inconsistent: saturated steam at 150 °C is at 476.0 kPa, so a figure or the label is wrong

choices.label: The entry is consistent, since wet steam can be at any pressure at one given temperature
Inconsistent: saturated steam at 150 °C is at 476.0 kPa, so a figure or the label is wrong
The entry is consistent, since 300 kPa lies well inside the range of pressures in the table
The pair is impossible, since at 300 kPa water at 150 °C would have to be a compressed liquid

questions.onCorrect: A saturated state at 150 °C has one pressure, 476.0 kPa, so the logged pair cannot both be right.

misconceptions.feedback: In the mixture region the pressure is tied to the temperature, so 150 °C allows only 476.0 kPa. Wet steam is a mixture of the saturated liquid and vapour.
Being inside the table's range of pressures does not make the pair a saturated state. At 150 °C only 476.0 kPa does.
Compressed liquid needs a pressure above the saturation pressure. At 300 kPa, which is below 476.0 kPa, water at 150 °C would be superheated vapour.

questions.prompt: Sort each state of water into its region. The table gives saturation pressures of 2.336 kPa at 20 °C, 198.50 kPa at 120 °C, 476.0 kPa at 150 °C, 1,554.3 kPa at 200 °C and 3,904.1 kPa at 248.9 °C.
hints: Look up the saturation pressure at each temperature, then compare it with the pressure given.
An item that gives both phases present is already a mixture, and its pressure should match the table.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compressed liquid: 20 °C at 101 kPa and 150 °C at 2,000 kPa. Superheated vapour: 120 °C at 101 kPa and 250 °C at 1,000 kPa. Mixture: the two saturated states.

items.label: 20 °C at 101 kPa
items.explanation: The saturation pressure at 20 °C is 2.336 kPa, so water at 101 kPa is under much more pressure than it needs to stay liquid.

items.label: 150 °C at 2,000 kPa
items.explanation: The saturation pressure at 150 °C is 476.0 kPa, and 2,000 kPa is above it.

items.label: 120 °C at 101 kPa
items.explanation: The saturation pressure at 120 °C is 198.50 kPa, and 101 kPa is below it, so the water is above its boiling point.

items.label: 250 °C at 1,000 kPa
items.explanation: The saturation pressure is already 3,904.1 kPa at 248.9 °C, far above 1,000 kPa, so water at 250 °C and 1,000 kPa is above its boiling point.

items.label: 200 °C at 1,554.3 kPa, with liquid and vapour both present
items.explanation: The pair is the table's saturation pair, and both phases are present, so it is a mixture.

items.label: 40 °C at 7.370 kPa, with 60% of the mass as vapour
items.explanation: The pair is the table's saturation pair, and the quality of 0.60 places it inside the mixture region.

questions.onCorrect: Pressure above saturation gives compressed liquid, pressure below it gives superheated vapour, and the saturation pair with both phases present is a mixture.

questions.prompt: A sealed rigid tank of air reads 150 kPa on its gauge at 25 °C, and the atmosphere is 101.3 kPa. The tank is heated to 125 °C. What does the gauge read now, in kPa? (K = °C + 273.)
hints: Convert the pressure and both temperatures to absolute values first.
In a rigid sealed tank the absolute pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature.
Scale the absolute pressure, then convert back to a gauge reading.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Absolute pressure is 150 + 101.3 = 251.3 kPa at 298 K. At 398 K it is 251.3 × 398/298 = 335.6 kPa, so the gauge reads 335.6 − 101.3 = 234.3 kPa.

questions.onCorrect: The absolute pressure rises from 251.3 to 335.6 kPa, and subtracting the atmosphere gives a gauge reading of 234.3 kPa.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the gauge reading by the Celsius figures, 125/25. Both the pressure and the temperature must be absolute.
That scales the gauge reading by the kelvin ratio. The ratio applies to the absolute pressure, which includes the atmosphere.
That scales the gauge reading by the kelvin ratio. The ratio applies to the absolute pressure, which includes the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: A design note estimates the density of saturated steam at 200 °C and 1,554.3 kPa from $Pv = RT$ and gets 7.12 kg/m³. The steam table gives 7.868 kg/m³ at that state. What should the engineer conclude?
hints: Work out the percentage difference between the two densities.
Ask which of the two figures is a model and which is a tabulated property.

acceptedIdeas: The gas law is about 10% low here, so the table's density should be used
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gas law is about 10% low here, so the table's density should be used

choices.label: The two agree closely enough, since both are about 7 kg/m³
The gas law is about 10% high here, so its value is a conservative figure
The table must be wrong, since steam above 100 °C obeys the gas law exactly
The gas law is about 10% low here, so the table's density should be used

questions.onCorrect: Near saturation at 1,554.3 kPa the gas law understates the density by about 10%, so the table is the figure to use.

misconceptions.feedback: The two differ by about 10%, which is far more than the rounding of the figures and enough to change a design.
The gas law's figure is the smaller one, 7.12 against 7.868, so it is about 10% low and not high.
No real gas obeys the gas law exactly, and steam near saturation at 1,554.3 kPa is a clear case. The table values are the measured ones.

questions.prompt: Steam enters a turbine carrying 3,100 kJ of energy for each kilogram and leaves carrying 2,500 kJ for each kilogram. The casing is perfectly insulated, so no heat crosses it. How much work does each kilogram of steam deliver, in kJ?
hints: Energy is conserved, and the only things that cross the boundary are the steam and the shaft.
Whatever energy each kilogram loses must appear as work on the shaft.
Subtract the energy carried out from the energy carried in.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no heat crossing, the energy lost by each kilogram of steam is the work: 3,100 − 2,500 = 600 kJ.

questions.onCorrect: Each kilogram delivers 600 kJ, the difference between the energy it carries in and the energy it carries out.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two figures. Work is the energy that the steam loses, which is the difference between them.

questions.prompt: Why can the potential energy at the outlet be left out of this balance?
hints: Height is always measured from some chosen level.
Only the difference in height between the inlet and the outlet matters.

acceptedIdeas: The outlet is the zero of height, so only the inlet's 2 m counts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The outlet is the zero of height, so only the inlet's 2 m counts

choices.label: The outlet is the zero of height, so only the inlet's 2 m counts
Because a turbine cannot change the height of the steam passing through it
Because the potential energy of steam is negligible in every machine

questions.onCorrect: Choosing the outlet as the zero of height puts all of the 2 m difference into the inlet term.

misconceptions.feedback: Height is measured from a level that is chosen freely, and the steam does end up 2 m lower. What matters is the difference between inlet and outlet.
Its size is small here, as the next screen shows, but that is a separate point. The outlet term is missing because that level was chosen as zero.

questions.prompt: Steam enters a turbine at 3,230 kJ/kg and leaves at 2,420 kJ/kg, and 15 kJ of heat is lost through the casing for each kilogram. Ignoring the changes in speed and height, what work does each kilogram deliver, in kJ?
hints: Write the balance per kilogram with the speed and height terms left out.
The enthalpy falls by 810 kJ/kg, and some of that leaves as heat.
Subtract the heat lost from the enthalpy drop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: w = h1 − h2 + q, with q = −15 kJ/kg for heat lost: 3,230 − 2,420 − 15 = 795 kJ/kg.

questions.onCorrect: The enthalpy drop is 810 kJ/kg, and 15 kJ/kg of it leaves as heat, so 795 kJ/kg reaches the shaft.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole enthalpy drop. Some of it leaves as heat through the casing, so less reaches the shaft.
That adds the heat loss to the enthalpy drop. Heat leaving the steam reduces the work, so it is subtracted.

questions.prompt: Refrigerant passes through a throttle valve, and its pressure drops. Which quantity does the ideal analysis keep constant?
hints: Write the balance for a valve: which of the heat and work terms is zero?
Speed and height changes are small, so what remains on the two sides?

acceptedIdeas: Its enthalpy, because no work or heat crosses the valve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its enthalpy, because no work or heat crosses the valve

choices.label: Its temperature, because no heat crosses the valve
Its pressure, because the valve sits in a pipe at steady flow
Its enthalpy, because no work or heat crosses the valve

questions.onCorrect: With no shaft and no heat, and speed and height changes small, the balance leaves $h_1 = h_2$.

misconceptions.feedback: No heat crossing does not hold the temperature fixed. The fluid can cool as it expands, and a refrigerator's valve relies on that. What stays fixed is the enthalpy.
Pressure is what the valve changes, and it drops abruptly. Steady flow means the flow rate does not change with time.

questions.prompt: A student finds the heat that a condenser removes from the steam as $\dot m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ over the 10 K of subcooling, and gets about 42 kJ for each kilogram of steam. The enthalpies give 2,448 kJ/kg. What went wrong?
hints: During condensation the steam stays at one temperature, so $\Delta T$ is zero for that part.

acceptedIdeas: It missed the latent heat released while the steam condensed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It missed the latent heat released while the steam condensed

choices.label: The specific heat of water was out by a factor of about ten
The subcooling was counted once, but each side of the exchanger needs it twice
It missed the latent heat released while the steam condensed

questions.onCorrect: The temperature barely moves while steam condenses, so $c_p\,\Delta T$ misses the latent heat, which is nearly all of the heat.

misconceptions.feedback: A value near 4.18 kJ/(kg K) is right for liquid water. The shortfall is a factor of about 58, and no error in $c_p$ explains that.
Subcooling happens on the steam side only. Doubling 42 kJ/kg would still miss nearly all of the 2,448 kJ/kg.

questions.prompt: Steam flows through a condenser at 555.6 kg/s, entering at 2,574 kJ/kg and leaving as liquid at 125.8 kJ/kg. At what rate does it give up heat, in kW?
hints: Find the enthalpy that each kilogram of steam gives up.
Multiply by the number of kilograms each second.
One kJ per second is one kW.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each kilogram gives up 2,574 − 125.8 = 2,448.2 kJ, so the rate is 555.6 × 2,448.2 = 1,360,000 kW, about 1.36 GW.

questions.onCorrect: The steam gives up 2,448.2 kJ for each kilogram, and at 555.6 kg/s that is 1.36 million kW.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $\dot m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ over the 10 K of subcooling alone. It leaves out the latent heat released as the steam condenses.
That is $\dot m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ over the 10 K of subcooling alone. It leaves out the latent heat released as the steam condenses.
That is the heat for one kilogram. Multiply by the steam flow in kg/s to get the rate.

questions.prompt: The condenser gives up heat at 1,360,000 kW, and each kilogram of cooling water gains 29.3 kJ as it warms from 18 °C to 25 °C. What mass flow of cooling water does it need, in kg/s?
hints: The water gains all the heat that the steam loses.
Heat rate equals mass flow times the enthalpy gained per kilogram.
Divide the heat rate by 29.3 kJ/kg.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The water must take up all the heat, so the flow is 1,360,000 ÷ 29.3 = 46,400 kg/s.

questions.onCorrect: The cooling water needs 46,400 kg/s, which is about 84 kg of water for each kilogram of steam.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio of water to steam for one kilogram. The flow is that heat rate divided by the gain per kilogram.
That multiplies the heat rate by 29.3. The flow is the heat rate divided by the gain per kilogram.

questions.prompt: A river can supply 20,000 kg/s of cooling water at 18 °C (75.6 kJ/kg), which may leave at 25 °C (104.9 kJ/kg). The steam enters the condenser at 2,574 kJ/kg and leaves at 125.8 kJ/kg. What steam flow can this condenser handle, in kg/s?
hints: The water gains 29.3 kJ per kilogram, so find the heat it can take up each second.
The steam must give up exactly that much heat.
Divide by the 2,448.2 kJ that each kilogram of steam gives up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The water can take up 20,000 × 29.3 = 586,000 kW. Each kilogram of steam gives up 2,448.2 kJ, so the steam flow is 586,000 ÷ 2,448.2 = 239.4 kg/s.

questions.onCorrect: The river can absorb 586,000 kW, which condenses 239.4 kg/s of this steam.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the other way round. The water flow is the larger one, and the steam flow is the water's heat uptake divided by the steam's heat per kilogram.
That divides the other way round. The water flow is the larger one, and the steam flow is the water's heat uptake divided by the steam's heat per kilogram.

questions.prompt: A river authority relaxes its discharge limit, so that the cooling water may leave at 30 °C (125.6 kJ/kg) instead of 25 °C (104.9 kJ/kg). It still enters at 18 °C (75.6 kJ/kg), and the condenser's steam load is the same. What happens to the cooling water flow that it needs?
hints: The heat to be removed is unchanged. What does each kilogram of water now carry away?

choices.label: It rises by about 70%, because a hotter exit needs more water to hold the same heat
It stays the same, because the steam gives up the same heat as before
It falls by about 40%, because each kilogram now gains 50.0 kJ instead of 29.3 kJ
It falls by about 15%, because 30 °C is only 5 K above the old limit

misconceptions.feedback: A larger gain per kilogram means fewer kilograms for the same heat, so the flow falls. Each kilogram now gains 50.0 kJ instead of 29.3 kJ.
The heat is the same, but the water flow is that heat divided by the gain per kilogram, and the gain per kilogram is now larger.
The gain per kilogram rises from 29.3 to 50.0 kJ, which is 71% more, since the rise in temperature goes from 7 K to 12 K. The flow falls by 41%.

questions.prompt: A turbine must deliver 100 MW. Steam enters at 3,350 kJ/kg and leaves at 2,300 kJ/kg, and the casing is well insulated, so heat loss can be taken as zero. Ignoring changes in speed and height, what steam flow does it need, in kg/s?
hints: First find the work that each kilogram delivers.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each kilogram delivers 3,350 − 2,300 = 1,050 kJ, so 100 MW, which is 100,000 kJ/s, needs 100,000 ÷ 1,050 = 95.2 kg/s.

questions.onCorrect: Each kilogram gives 1,050 kJ, so 100,000 kJ/s needs a flow of 95.2 kg/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the work from each kilogram. The question asks for the flow that gives 100 MW.
That divides the work per kilogram by the power. The flow is the power divided by the work per kilogram.

questions.prompt: Steam enters a nozzle at 20 m/s and leaves at 600 m/s while its enthalpy falls by 180 kJ/kg. Which statement about the energy balance is right?
hints: Work out the change in kinetic energy per kilogram, $(V_2^2 - V_1^2)/2$, in kJ/kg.
Compare it with the enthalpy change.

acceptedIdeas: The kinetic energy term must stay, since it is as large as the enthalpy change
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kinetic energy term must stay, since it is as large as the enthalpy change

choices.label: The kinetic energy term can be dropped, since speed terms are negligible in every machine
The enthalpy term can be dropped, since the speed changes by a factor of thirty
The kinetic energy term can be dropped, since a nozzle has no shaft work
The kinetic energy term must stay, since it is as large as the enthalpy change

questions.onCorrect: The kinetic energy rises by about 180 kJ/kg, which is the whole enthalpy drop, so it is the point of the machine.

misconceptions.feedback: The speed term is negligible in a turbine because it is tiny beside the enthalpy drop. Here the speed change is 180 kJ/kg, the same size as the enthalpy change.
The enthalpy change is the largest term that supplies the speed, and the balance cannot work without it. Dropping it leaves nothing to account for the new speed.
Having no shaft work removes the work term, and the kinetic energy term stays. The change in speed is the purpose of a nozzle.

questions.prompt: An engineer measures the heat that a condenser's cooling water gains and finds it is only 90% of the heat that the steam loses. Which explanation fits the first law?
hints: The first law says energy is conserved, so ask where else the energy can go.

choices.label: A tenth of the energy was destroyed when the steam condensed
The latent heat is not available to the water, which takes up only the subcooling
Heat leaks through the shell to the air, or the readings are slightly out
The steam does work on the cooling water, which accounts for the missing tenth

questions.onCorrect: The shell is warmer than the surroundings, so some heat leaks out of the condenser. The first law accounts for it, and the cooling water gains less than the steam loses.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy is neither created nor destroyed. Heat that does not reach the water has gone somewhere else, or the readings are slightly out.

questions.prompt: What is the highest efficiency that any engine could reach between a source at 600 °C and a sink at 25 °C, in percent? (K = °C + 273.)
hints: The limit is one minus the ratio of the two temperatures.
Both temperatures must be in kelvin before you take the ratio.
Write the result as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The Carnot limit between 873 K and 298 K is 65.9%, and no engine between those temperatures can exceed it.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the Celsius figures, 1 − 25/600. The ratio needs absolute temperatures, with zero at absolute zero.

questions.prompt: A power plant raises steam at 450 °C and cools it with water at 40 °C. What is the Carnot efficiency between those temperatures, in percent? (K = °C + 273.)
hints: Convert both temperatures to kelvin first.
Take the ratio of the sink to the source.
Subtract the ratio from one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T_H = 450 + 273 = 723 K and T_C = 40 + 273 = 313 K, so the efficiency is 1 − 313/723 = 0.567, which is 56.7%.

questions.onCorrect: Between 723 K and 313 K the limit is 56.7%, so a plant at those temperatures can never do better.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the Celsius figures, 1 − 40/450. Convert both temperatures to kelvin first.
That is the ratio $T_C/T_H$ itself. The limit is one minus that ratio.

questions.prompt: Why must the temperatures be converted to kelvin before the limit is worked out?
hints: A ratio of temperatures is meaningful only if zero means no thermal energy.
Where does the Celsius scale put its zero?

acceptedIdeas: The limit uses absolute temperatures, and Celsius puts zero at the freezing point
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit uses absolute temperatures, and Celsius puts zero at the freezing point

choices.label: The limit uses absolute temperatures, and Celsius puts zero at the freezing point
Kelvin figures are larger, which makes the result of the formula easier to read off
The Celsius scale does not apply to steam, since steam is hotter than the 100 °C boiling point

questions.onCorrect: A ratio needs a true zero, and only the absolute scale has one.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the numbers is not the point. A ratio of Celsius values is a different number, and for a 25 °C sink it comes out nearly 12 times too small.
The Celsius scale works at any temperature. It is a ratio, not a difference, that needs a true zero, and Celsius has an arbitrary one.

questions.prompt: A steam source is at 171 °C and heat is rejected at 16 °C. What is the Carnot efficiency between them, in percent? (K = °C + 273.)
hints: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
Take the ratio of the sink to the source.
Subtract the ratio from one and write it as a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The limit between 444 K and 289 K is 34.9%, which is about 35%.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the Celsius figures, 1 − 16/171. Convert to kelvin first.
That is the ratio $T_C/T_H$ itself. The limit is one minus that ratio.

questions.prompt: A steam cycle between 171 °C and 16 °C reaches an efficiency of 18.0%, and its Carnot limit is 34.9%. What percentage of its limit does it reach?
hints: Compare the actual efficiency with the limit by dividing one by the other.
Which one goes on top: what it reaches, or what it could reach?
Write the ratio as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The fraction is 18.0 ÷ 34.9 = 0.516, so the cycle reaches 51.6% of its limit.

questions.onCorrect: The cycle reaches about half of its limit, 51.6%.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the limit by the actual efficiency. The question asks what share of the limit the cycle reaches.
That subtracts the two efficiencies, 34.9 − 18.0. The question asks for a share, which is a ratio.

questions.prompt: An inventor says an engine takes 100 kJ of heat from a source at 450 K, rejects heat at 300 K and delivers 40 kJ of work. What is the verdict?
hints: Work out the Carnot limit for 450 K and 300 K.
Compare the claimed efficiency, work divided by heat in, with that limit.

acceptedIdeas: Not possible: 40% is above the limit of 33.3% for those temperatures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not possible: 40% is above the limit of 33.3% for those temperatures

choices.label: Possible, since 40% is well below the 100% that is the highest figure possible
Possible, since the engine rejects 60 kJ and the first law balances
Possible, if the engine is insulated better than a normal one
Not possible: 40% is above the limit of 33.3% for those temperatures

questions.onCorrect: The claim is 40% and the Carnot limit is 33.3%, so no design could meet it.

misconceptions.feedback: No engine between two temperatures comes near 100%. The limit here is 1 − 300/450, which is 33.3%.
The first law is satisfied, but it says nothing about the direction of the process. The second law caps this engine at 33.3% and the claim is 40%.
Insulation reduces heat that leaks away, and it cannot raise an engine above its second-law cap of 33.3%.

questions.prompt: A vendor claims 52% for an engine working between a 540 °C source and a 30 °C sink, for which the Carnot limit is 62.7%. What is the fair verdict?
hints: Is 52% above or below the Carnot limit of 62.7%?
What share of their limits did the real engines in this lesson reach?

acceptedIdeas: Allowed by the law, but far above the half of the limit that real engines usually reach
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Allowed by the law, but far above the half of the limit that real engines usually reach

choices.label: Impossible, since the second law makes every engine lose more than half of its heat
Plausible, since 52% is below the Carnot limit and the limit is the only test that applies
Allowed by the law, but far above the half of the limit that real engines usually reach
Plausible, since the Celsius figures give a limit of 94.4% and the claim is far below

questions.onCorrect: The claim passes the second-law test and is 83% of the limit, far beyond the roughly half that real engines reach, so it needs evidence.

misconceptions.feedback: No law sets the cap at one half. The cap is the Carnot limit, 62.7% here, and 52% is below it.
Being below the limit shows only that the claim is not impossible. Real engines reach about half of their limit, and 52% is 83% of this one.
The Celsius figures give a wrong limit. With absolute temperatures the limit is 62.7%.

questions.prompt: Burning fuel can reach about 1,670 °C, yet a steam plant holds its steam below about 816 °C. Why do plants not simply run hotter?
hints: Ask whether the cap gets better or worse as the source gets hotter.
Then ask what the boiler tubes are made of.

acceptedIdeas: Boiler metals cannot survive steam that hot, so the materials limit the source
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Boiler metals cannot survive steam that hot, so the materials limit the source

choices.label: The second law rules out any source temperature as high as that of burning fuel
Carnot efficiency falls as the source gets hotter, so a cooler source is the better one
The sink temperature would have to rise along with the source, which cancels the gain
Boiler metals cannot survive steam that hot, so the materials limit the source

questions.onCorrect: A hotter source would raise the limit, but boiler metals cannot hold steam above about 816 °C, so materials set the source limit.

misconceptions.feedback: The law sets no limit on the source temperature. Its cap, $1 - T_C/T_H$, keeps rising as the source gets hotter.
It rises. The ratio $T_C/T_H$ shrinks as $T_H$ grows, so the limit grows. A hotter source would help if the boiler could stand it.
The sink is set by the environment, at about 16 °C, and it does not change with the source temperature.

questions.prompt: A handbook gives this statement of the second law, credited to Max Planck. Which proposed machine does it rule out?
hints: Find the one machine whose only effect is cooling one reservoir and doing work.
Which machines in the list reject heat to a second reservoir?

extracts.text: It is impossible to construct an engine that will work in a complete cycle and produce no other effect except the raising of a weight and the cooling of a heat reservoir.
extracts.who: U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Fundamentals Handbook: Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Flow, Volume 1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92)
extracts.kind: A US government fundamentals handbook for plant operators

acceptedIdeas: A ship's engine that takes heat from the sea, turns all of it into work and rejects none
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A ship's engine that takes heat from the sea, turns all of it into work and rejects none

choices.label: A refrigerator that uses electrical work to move heat from a cold box into a warm kitchen
A resistance heater that turns electrical work completely into heat
A ship's engine that takes heat from the sea, turns all of it into work and rejects none
An engine that rejects most of its heat to a river and delivers a little work

questions.onCorrect: A cycle that takes heat from the sea alone and turns all of it into work does nothing else, which is exactly what the statement forbids.

misconceptions.feedback: Work is supplied, so the machine has an effect beyond cooling a reservoir and raising a weight. Moving heat from cold to hot with work added is allowed.
Work can be turned completely into heat, as friction does. The handbook notes that the converse is never true for a cycle.
It rejects heat, so it does more than cool a reservoir and raise a weight. The passage rules out only an engine whose sole effect is that.

questions.prompt: Sort each statement by where the limit comes from: the second law, the environment or materials.
hints: Ask which statements would stay true for any engine in any place.
A limit that depends on a number, such as 16 °C or 816 °C, comes from the place or the hardware.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Law: no cycle converts all its heat and no engine beats a reversible one. Environment: the 16 °C sink and the surroundings. Materials: the boiler metals and the fuel temperature that tubes cannot take.

items.label: No cycle can turn all of its heat into work

items.label: Heat is finally rejected to the earth at about 16 °C
items.explanation: The earth is the final heat sink, so the cold end of any plant is fixed near its temperature.

items.label: Boiler metals cap the steam at about 816 °C

questions.prompt: A designer wants a Carnot limit of 45% with the sink at 300 K. What is the lowest source temperature that gives it, in K?

That divides by 0.45 itself. The ratio $T_C/T_H$ is 1 − 0.45, which is 0.55.

questions.prompt: Steam entering a turbine at 3,100 kJ/kg would deliver 360 kJ for each kilogram in an ideal expansion to the exhaust pressure. The real turbine delivers 262 kJ for each kilogram, and its casing loses almost no heat. Where did the other 98 kJ go?
hints: The first law says energy is conserved, so the 98 kJ has to be somewhere.

acceptedIdeas: It stays in the steam, which leaves with a higher enthalpy than the ideal exit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays in the steam, which leaves with a higher enthalpy than the ideal exit

choices.label: Friction in the blades destroys it as the steam passes through
It leaves through the casing as heat, which is most of the loss in a large machine
It stays in the steam, which leaves with a higher enthalpy than the ideal exit

questions.onCorrect: The energy is not lost. It stays in the exhaust, which leaves at a higher enthalpy than the ideal expansion would have given.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy is not destroyed. Friction turns the work that would have been delivered into thermal energy, and that energy stays in the steam.

questions.prompt: Why does the actual work go on top of the ratio when the efficiency of a turbine is worked out?
hints: Ask what a turbine is for, and what share of the best case it achieves.

acceptedIdeas: A turbine exists to deliver work, so the efficiency is the share of the ideal work it does

Because the actual work is always the larger of the two, and a ratio puts the larger on top
Because the ideal turbine is only a model and cannot be put on the bottom of a ratio

questions.prompt: A turbine has an isentropic efficiency of 0.85, and an ideal expansion of the same steam would deliver 360 kJ/kg. What work does the real turbine deliver, in kJ/kg?

questions.onCorrect: A real turbine delivers 0.85 of the ideal work, which is 306 kJ/kg.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the efficiency, which is how a pump is treated. A turbine delivers less work than an ideal one, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Steam enters a turbine at 3,100 kJ/kg, and the turbine delivers 306 kJ/kg with no heat loss. At what enthalpy does the steam leave, in kJ/kg?

The answer should lie above the ideal exit at 2,740 kJ/kg.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no heat loss the work is the enthalpy drop, so the exit enthalpy is 3,100 − 306 = 2,794 kJ/kg.

questions.onCorrect: The steam leaves at 2,794 kJ/kg, which is 54 kJ/kg above the ideal exit at 2,740 kJ/kg.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exit of the ideal expansion. The real steam leaves at a higher enthalpy, because less work was taken out.
That adds the work to the inlet enthalpy. The steam gives up the work, so its enthalpy falls.

questions.prompt: A feed pump needs 6.7 kJ/kg of work where an ideal pump would need 5.0 kJ/kg. Which figure is the pump's isentropic efficiency?
hints: A real pump needs more work than the ideal pump, and an efficiency cannot exceed 1.
Which of the two works goes on top to keep the ratio below 1?

acceptedIdeas: 0.75, the ideal work divided by the actual work
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.75, the ideal work divided by the actual work

choices.label: 1.33, the actual work divided by the ideal work
0.25, the share of the actual work that is wasted
0.75, the ideal work divided by the actual work

questions.onCorrect: A pump's efficiency is the ideal work divided by the actual work, 5.0 ÷ 6.7, which is 0.75.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the actual work on top, as for a turbine, which gives a figure above 1. A pump needs more work than an ideal one, so its ratio is the other way up.
That is the share of the pump's work that is wasted, 1.7 out of 6.7. It is 1 minus the efficiency, and the efficiency itself is the share that is useful.

questions.prompt: A feed pump with an isentropic efficiency of 0.80 takes in water at 167.2 kJ/kg. An ideal pump would raise the enthalpy by 8.0 kJ/kg. At what enthalpy does the real pump deliver the water, in kJ/kg?
hints: The real pump needs more work than the ideal one.
Divide the ideal rise by the efficiency to find the actual rise.
Add the actual rise to the inlet enthalpy.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The actual rise is the ideal rise divided by the efficiency: 8.0 ÷ 0.80 = 10.0 kJ/kg, so the exit enthalpy is 167.2 + 10.0 = 177.2 kJ/kg.

questions.onCorrect: The real pump raises the enthalpy by 10.0 kJ/kg and not 8.0, so the water leaves at 177.2 kJ/kg.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the ideal rise by the efficiency, as for a turbine. A pump needs more work than the ideal, so divide.
That is the exit of the ideal pump, 167.2 + 8.0. The real pump needs more work and delivers warmer water.
That is the rise in enthalpy, not the exit enthalpy. Add it to the inlet enthalpy.

questions.prompt: Two turbines expand the same steam from the same inlet state to the same exhaust pressure. On a temperature-entropy diagram, turbine A's exit lies further to the right than turbine B's. Which statement is right?
hints: A vertical line is the ideal expansion, with the entropy unchanged.
Further to the right means more entropy created. What does that do to the exit enthalpy and the work?

acceptedIdeas: A delivers less work, because more entropy was created inside it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A delivers less work, because more entropy was created inside it

choices.label: A delivers more work, because its steam leaves with the higher entropy
A and B deliver the same work, because both expand to the same pressure
B is an ideal turbine, since its exit lies nearer the vertical line
A delivers less work, because more entropy was created inside it

questions.onCorrect: A further-right exit means more entropy was created by losses, so the steam leaves with more of its energy and the turbine delivers less work.

misconceptions.feedback: More entropy at the exit means more entropy was created inside the machine. That comes from losses, and the further right the exit, the less work was taken out.
The same pressures fix the ideal expansion only. The real exit state, and the work, depend on how much entropy the machine creates.
An ideal turbine lies exactly on the vertical line. B is nearer to it, but it still leans to the right, so it still creates entropy.

questions.prompt: A data sheet lists an isentropic efficiency of 0.93 for a small 1 MW steam turbine and 0.78 for a large 500 MW unit. What is the fair reading?
hints: Recall the typical ranges for small turbines and for large ones.
Compare each figure with the range for its size.

acceptedIdeas: Both look swapped: small turbines run 60% to 80% and large ones about 90%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both look swapped: small turbines run 60% to 80% and large ones about 90%

choices.label: Both are plausible, since efficiency does not depend on a turbine's size
Only the 0.93 is doubtful, since 0.78 is typical of every size of turbine
Both are impossible, since no real turbine can exceed an efficiency of 0.75
Both look swapped: small turbines run 60% to 80% and large ones about 90%

questions.onCorrect: Small turbines are generally 60% to 80% and large ones about 90%, so the two figures are reversed and need checking.

misconceptions.feedback: The handbook gives 60% to 80% for small turbines and about 90% for large ones, so size does matter and the two figures look reversed.
The 0.78 is low for a large unit, which should be near 0.90, as well as the 0.93 being high for a small one.
No law caps the isentropic efficiency at 0.75, and the handbook gives large turbines at about 0.90.

questions.prompt: Steam enters a turbine at 3,350 kJ/kg. An ideal expansion to the exhaust pressure would end at 2,400 kJ/kg, and the real turbine's exhaust leaves at 2,550 kJ/kg. What is its isentropic efficiency?
hints: Find the enthalpy drop for the real turbine and for the ideal one.
Divide the actual drop by the ideal drop.
The result is below 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The actual drop is 3,350 − 2,550 = 800 kJ/kg and the ideal drop is 3,350 − 2,400 = 950 kJ/kg, so the efficiency is 800 ÷ 950 = 0.84.

questions.onCorrect: The real turbine takes out 800 of the ideal 950 kJ/kg, an efficiency of 0.84.

misconceptions.feedback: That puts the ideal drop on top. A turbine's efficiency is the actual work over the ideal work, so it is below 1.
That is the fraction of the ideal work that is lost. The efficiency is the fraction delivered.

questions.prompt: Sort each case by its cause of irreversibility.
hints: Ask which of the four causes each case would show if you followed the energy.
A fluid losing pressure with no work recovered is expansion, and two streams meeting directly are mixing.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Friction: the blades and the bearing. Unrestrained expansion: the valve and the burst pipe. Heat transfer through a finite temperature difference: the flue gas. Mixing: the open feedwater heater.

bins.label: Heat transfer through a finite temperature difference

items.label: Steam rubbing along turbine blades
items.explanation: The rubbing turns work into thermal energy in the steam.

items.label: Oil dragging in a bearing
items.explanation: A moving surface rubbing against another is friction.

items.label: Steam passing through a partly closed valve
items.explanation: The pressure falls and no work is recovered, so the expansion is unrestrained.

items.label: Compressed gas escaping from a burst pipe into the open air
items.explanation: The gas expands freely without doing work.

items.label: Flue gas at 1,000 °C heating water at 200 °C across a tube wall
items.explanation: The heat crosses a gap of hundreds of kelvin.

items.label: Cool feedwater joining hotter steam in an open feedwater heater
items.explanation: The two streams are combined directly, which is mixing.

questions.onCorrect: Rubbing is friction, a pressure drop without work is unrestrained expansion, a large temperature gap is heat transfer, and direct combining is mixing.

questions.prompt: A steam plant's turbine and feed pump each have an isentropic efficiency of 0.80. An ideal expansion in the turbine would deliver 360 kJ/kg, and an ideal pump would need 5.0 kJ/kg. The plant can raise only one of the two to 0.85. Which gains more net work for each kilogram of steam?
hints: Work out the extra turbine work from a rise of 0.05 in efficiency.
Then work out how much less work the pump would need.

acceptedIdeas: The turbine, which gains 18 kJ/kg, while the pump would save only about 0.4 kJ/kg
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turbine, which gains 18 kJ/kg, while the pump would save only about 0.4 kJ/kg

choices.label: The pump, because the same gain in efficiency saves a larger share of its work
They gain the same, since both efficiencies rise by 0.05
Neither, because a rise of 0.05 in efficiency changes the net work by only 0.05 kJ/kg
The turbine, which gains 18 kJ/kg, while the pump would save only about 0.4 kJ/kg

questions.onCorrect: The turbine gains 0.05 × 360 = 18 kJ/kg, and the pump would save only 5.0/0.80 − 5.0/0.85 = 0.4 kJ/kg, so the turbine is the better upgrade.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger share of a small amount is still small. The pump's work falls by about 0.4 kJ/kg, against 18 kJ/kg gained at the turbine.
The same rise in efficiency applies to very different amounts of ideal work, 360 kJ/kg and 5.0 kJ/kg, so the gains differ greatly.
Efficiency multiplies the ideal work, so a rise of 0.05 on 360 kJ/kg is 18 kJ/kg. The change is not 0.05 kJ/kg.

questions.prompt: A steam plant's condenser delivers saturated liquid at 40 °C and 7.37 kPa to the feed pump, which raises it to the boiler pressure. In what state does the water leave the pump?
hints: At 7.37 kPa water boils at 40 °C. What happens to the boiling temperature when the pressure is raised?
Compare the water's temperature, still close to 40 °C, with the boiling temperature at the boiler pressure. Which side of it is the water on?

acceptedIdeas: Compressed liquid, since 40 °C is far below the boiling point at that pressure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compressed liquid, since 40 °C is far below the boiling point at that pressure

questions.onCorrect: Compressed liquid: at the boiler pressure the boiling point is far above 40 °C, so the pump leaves the water liquid.

misconceptions.feedback: Raising the pressure raises the boiling point as well, so water at about 40 °C stays a long way below it. Turning it into steam is the boiler's job.
A pump adds only a small amount of energy to a liquid, far too little to bring the water up to its boiling point at the boiler pressure.

choices.label: Steam, since a higher pressure gives the water more energy in every kilogram
A liquid and vapour mixture, since the pump's work brings the water to its boiling point
Compressed liquid, since 40 °C is far below the boiling point at that pressure

questions.prompt: In the worked cycle the net work came out as 1,185.2 kJ/kg from the turbine and the pump, and again as 3,218.0 - 2,032.8 from the boiler and the condenser. Why must the two agree?
hints: Over one whole cycle the water returns to state 1. What does that say about its energy change?
Apply the first law to the whole loop: energy in as heat and pump work, energy out as heat and turbine work.

acceptedIdeas: The water ends the cycle in its starting state, so its energy has not changed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The water ends the cycle in its starting state, so its energy has not changed

questions.onCorrect: Round a complete cycle the energy of the water is unchanged, so net work equals the heat added less the heat removed.

misconceptions.feedback: The boiler adds 3,218.0 kJ/kg and the condenser removes only 2,032.8, so the two heats are not equal. The difference between them is the work.
Isentropic does not mean no energy exchange: the turbine delivers work and the pump takes it. It means the process is reversible with no heat transfer.

choices.label: The boiler and the condenser pass the same heat, so the net work is the difference of two equal terms
The pump and the turbine are isentropic, so they exchange no energy with the water
The water ends the cycle in its starting state, so its energy has not changed

questions.prompt: Cycle B has h1 = 167.2, h2 = 182.0, h3 = 3,500 and h4 = 2,250 kJ/kg. How much heat does the boiler add to each kilogram of water?
hints: The boiler sits between two numbered states. Which two?
The water reaches the boiler after the pump, not before it.

acceptedIdeas: 3,318.0 kJ/kg, the rise from the pump outlet to the turbine inlet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 3,318.0 kJ/kg, the rise from the pump outlet to the turbine inlet

questions.onCorrect: The boiler takes the water from state 2 to state 3, so its heat is $h_3 - h_2$.

misconceptions.feedback: That measures from state 1, but the water has been through the pump by the time it enters the boiler, so the boiler's heat is measured from $h_2$.
That is the turbine's work, a fall in enthalpy as work leaves the steam, and not the heat the boiler puts in.
That is $h_4 - h_1$, the heat the condenser removes. The boiler works between states 2 and 3.

choices.label: 3,332.8 kJ/kg, the rise from the condenser outlet to the turbine inlet
1,250.0 kJ/kg, the fall in enthalpy across the turbine
2,082.8 kJ/kg, the heat the condenser removes
3,318.0 kJ/kg, the rise from the pump outlet to the turbine inlet

questions.prompt: What is the thermal efficiency of cycle B, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Start from the net work, which is the turbine's work less the pump's.
Divide that by the heat the boiler adds, the figure you chose above.
A real single-cycle steam plant reaches 35 to 42%, so check that your answer lies in that range.
questions.onCorrect: Cycle B reaches 37.2%, a little above the 36.8% of the first cycle, and still inside the range of real single-cycle plants.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the pump. The net work is the turbine's work less the pump's, even though the pump's share is small.
That measures the boiler's heat from state 1. The water enters the boiler after the pump, so the heat is measured from state 2.
That divides by the heat the condenser removes. The efficiency compares the net work with the heat the boiler adds.

questions.prompt: A student's sheet for a steam cycle gives h1 = 167.2, h2 = 467.2, h3 = 3,400 and h4 = 2,200 kJ/kg, with the condenser at 40 °C and 7.37 kPa. Which entry is the likeliest mistake?
hints: Work out the pump work and the turbine work from the four entries.
Compare the pump work with the turbine work. The feed pump of a real steam plant takes 1 to 3% of the turbine's output.

acceptedIdeas: h2, because it makes the pump work a quarter of the turbine's
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: h2, because it makes the pump work a quarter of the turbine's

questions.onCorrect: The pump work would be 300 kJ/kg against 1,200 for the turbine, which is 25% where a liquid pump takes 1 to 3%.

misconceptions.feedback: 167.2 kJ/kg is exactly the table's value for saturated liquid at 40 °C.
Steam usually leaves a turbine wet. At 40 °C dry vapour would be 2,572 kJ/kg, and 2,200 puts the exhaust at a quality of 84.5%, a normal value.
The table lists saturated steam, which tops out near 2,800 kJ/kg. Steam heated beyond saturation carries more, and the steam entering a turbine is of that kind.

choices.label: h2, because it makes the pump work a quarter of the turbine's
h1, because it differs from the table value for liquid at 40 °C
h4, because steam leaves a turbine as dry vapour at that pressure
h3, because the steam table has no steam above 2,800 kJ/kg

questions.prompt: In summer the cooling water of a steam plant warms, and the condenser settles at a higher temperature and pressure. The boiler end of the cycle is unchanged. What happens to the thermal efficiency?
hints: Use $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$ and ask which way a larger $T_c$ moves it.
On the diagram a warmer condenser makes the grey rectangle taller. What does that do to the work area?

acceptedIdeas: It falls, because the cycle rejects its heat at a higher temperature
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, because the cycle rejects its heat at a higher temperature

questions.onCorrect: A warmer cold side narrows the temperature range the cycle works across, so the same heat yields less work.

misconceptions.feedback: More heat leaving is a loss, not a gain. The net work is the heat added less the heat rejected, and with $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$ a larger $T_c$ lowers the efficiency.
Efficiency depends on both ends of the cycle. In $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$ a higher $T_c$ lowers it even when the boiler end is unchanged.

choices.label: It falls, because the cycle rejects its heat at a higher temperature
It rises, because the hotter exhaust carries more energy out of the cycle
It stays the same, because the boiler end alone sets the efficiency

questions.prompt: The last-stage blades of a turbine that runs on saturated steam show pitting and erosion. Which change would reduce the damage and raise the efficiency at the same time?
hints: Droplets form when the expansion ends inside the wet region. Where would you want state 3 to be?
Which of the three changes raises the average heat-input temperature, and which lower the efficiency?

acceptedIdeas: Superheat the steam so that it enters the turbine above saturation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Superheat the steam so that it enters the turbine above saturation

questions.onCorrect: Superheating keeps the exhaust drier and raises the average heat-input temperature as well, which is why plants use it.

misconceptions.feedback: Subcooling lowers the cycle's efficiency, because the extra heat removed has to be put back in the boiler, and it does nothing for the steam inside the turbine.
A warmer condenser rejects heat at a higher temperature, which lowers the efficiency, so it fails the second half of the requirement.

choices.label: Cool the condensate below its saturation temperature in the condenser
Superheat the steam so that it enters the turbine above saturation
Run the condenser warmer so that the steam leaves the turbine hotter

questions.prompt: The DOE handbook describes a typical steam plant with reheat. Saturated steam leaves its steam generator at about 282 °C, and the high-pressure turbine leaves it at 82.5% quality. In what order does the water pass through these six stages, starting at the steam generator?
hints: Follow the steam from where it is made. After the first turbine it is wet. What has to happen to wet steam before it meets a second turbine?
The pumps come last because the water must be a liquid before it is pumped.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steam generator makes the steam, the high-pressure turbine expands it to 82.5% quality, the moisture separator and reheater dry it and heat it again, the low-pressure turbine expands it to the condenser pressure, the condenser turns it back into liquid, and the pumps with their feedwater heaters return it to the steam generator.

items: Steam generator, where heat is added at constant pressure
High-pressure turbine, which leaves the steam at 82.5% quality
Moisture separator and reheater, which dry the steam and heat it again
Condenser, where the heat goes to the cooling water
Condensate and feed pumps, with the feedwater heaters

questions.onCorrect: Drying the 17.5% of liquid between the two turbines lets the steam expand all the way to the condenser pressure without wearing the last blades.

questions.prompt: A designer taps some steam from the turbine to warm the water returning to the boiler. That steam no longer produces turbine work. Why does the efficiency of the plant still rise?
hints: Where does the boiler's heat now enter: at a low feedwater temperature or at a higher one?
Which of the two temperatures in $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$ does warming the feedwater act on?

acceptedIdeas: The boiler starts from hotter feedwater, so its heat enters at a higher temperature
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The boiler starts from hotter feedwater, so its heat enters at a higher temperature

questions.onCorrect: Warming the feedwater removes the low-temperature part of the boiler's heat, which raises the average heat-input temperature.

misconceptions.feedback: Pump work is only 1 to 3% of the turbine's output, so it cannot pay for the turbine work lost to the bled steam.
The condenser's temperature is set by its cooling water, not by the amount of steam that reaches it, and a colder condenser is not what regeneration provides.

choices.label: The feed pump needs less work, and that saving outweighs the turbine work lost
The condenser runs colder, because less steam reaches it and it needs less cooling
The boiler starts from hotter feedwater, so its heat enters at a higher temperature

questions.prompt: A steam cycle has a thermal efficiency of 40% and rejects its heat in a condenser at 40 °C (313 K). If the cycle is ideal, what is its average heat-input temperature, in kelvin?
hints: Rearrange $\eta = 1 - T_c / \bar T_{in}$ to find $\bar T_{in}$.
The ratio $T_c / \bar T_{in}$ equals $1 - \eta$, which is 0.60 here.
Divide the condenser temperature in kelvin by that ratio.
questions.onCorrect: About 522 K, or 249 °C, well below the 538 to 566 °C of the steam in a 40% plant, because the heat enters over a range that starts at the cold feedwater.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the Celsius temperature. The relation needs absolute temperatures, so work in kelvin.
That multiplies where the relation divides. The condenser temperature is a fraction of the average heat-input temperature, not a multiple of it.
That divides by the efficiency, 0.40. It is the ratio $T_c / \bar T_{in}$ that equals $1 - \eta$.

questions.prompt: A report on a steam plant makes six statements. Which are plausible, and which need checking before you rely on them?
hints: Compare each statement with a figure from the lesson: 35 to 42% for steam alone, 1 to 3% for the pump.
For the last statement, the net work is the heat added less the heat removed.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 40% and 42% plants and the 2% pump are in the usual ranges. A steam plant at 55%, a pump taking 20% of the turbine output and a condenser that removes more heat than the boiler adds are not.

items.label: A steam plant at 24.1 MPa and 540 °C reports a thermal efficiency of 40%
items.explanation: Plants at about 24.1 MPa and 538 to 566 °C reach about 40%.

items.label: A single-cycle steam plant reports a thermal efficiency of 55%
items.explanation: A steam plant on its own is limited to 35 to 42%.

items.label: A feed pump takes 2% of the turbine's output
items.explanation: Pumping a liquid takes 1 to 3% of the turbine's output.

items.label: A feed pump takes 20% of the turbine's output

items.label: A plant at 31 MPa and 600 °C reports a thermal efficiency of 42%
items.explanation: Ultra-supercritical plants at 31 MPa and 600 °C reach about 42%.

questions.prompt: The ideal Brayton efficiency is $1 - r_p^{-x}$, where $r_p$ is the pressure ratio and $\gamma = 1.4$ for air. What is the exponent $x$?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.286, which is $(\gamma - 1) / \gamma$

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reciprocal of the exponent. It would give an efficiency of almost 100% at any ratio, which no engine approaches.
That is $\gamma - 1$ on its own. For a pressure ratio the formula divides it by $\gamma$.

choices.label: 3.5, which is $\gamma / (\gamma - 1)$, the reciprocal
0.4, which is $\gamma - 1$ on its own

questions.prompt: What is the ideal efficiency of a gas turbine with a pressure ratio of 16 and $\gamma = 1.4$, as a percentage to one decimal place?
hints: Work out $16^{0.2857}$ first, with a calculator's power key or as $e^{0.2857 \ln 16}$.

Check your answer against the curve in the figure, where the point for a ratio of 16 is marked.

questions.prompt: A maker raises a gas turbine's firing temperature from 1,200 °C to 1,400 °C and keeps the pressure ratio the same. What happens to the ideal efficiency?
hints: Look at the formula for the ideal efficiency. Which quantities does it contain?
Is a temperature among them?

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same, since the formula contains only $r_p$ and $\gamma$
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays the same, since the formula contains only $r_p$ and $\gamma$

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel per kilogram of air raises the heat added and the work together, in the same proportion, so the ideal efficiency does not move.

choices.label: It falls, since more fuel is burned in each kilogram of air
It stays the same, since the formula contains only $r_p$ and $\gamma$
It rises, since a hotter source raises the Carnot limit for the engine

questions.prompt: A designer proposes raising a gas turbine's pressure ratio from 16 to 30, which would take the ideal efficiency from 54.7% to 62.2%. What is the main practical objection?
hints: What happens to the temperature of the air leaving the compressor as the pressure ratio rises?
